Sheet 1 / 11 · Unit 11e–11f · History

Aims of the lesson & Lead-in

Aims of the lesson

By the end of the lesson, you will be able to:

📚Remember · Understand
  • Name the words and chunks of the 4 groups: life stories, mountains and adventure, space exploration, messages and records.
  • Explain where the quotation marks, the comma and the full stop go in direct speech, and why we write said Kammerlander but not said he.
  • Recall Voyager 1’s mission and what the Golden Record carries: photos, sounds, music and greetings.
🛠️Apply · Analyse
  • Use was born, the past simple, the present perfect and famous for + -ing in the right places in a life story.
  • Analyse The world’s greatest mountaineer: which paragraph gives Messner’s birth, his fame, his own words, other people’s views and his life now.
  • Find numbers, facts and reasons in the two Golden Record videos and in the PET Reading and Listening extras.
💡Evaluate · Create
  • Compose a short spoken portrait of someone you admire, quoting their words in correct direct speech.
  • Evaluate a documentary you have seen (Topic 9) or an important event in Vietnam’s history (Topic 4) with the 7-step frame.
  • Write a single paragraph on the benefits and drawbacks of exploring space, ending with a clear judgement.

Lead-in 1 · A climber, a spacecraft and a golden record — look, guess and react

4:00Take turns: one of you picks a picture, the other asks its three questions.
A man on a mountain rock
  1. Question 1
    ‘Who do you think this man is? Look at his clothes and the place for clues.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Climbers like him go above 8,000 metres, sometimes with no oxygen tanks. What happens to the human body up there?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Would you follow him up a dangerous peak if he invited you? Why or why not?’
A spacecraft passing a giant planet
  1. Question 1
    ‘Can you name the striped planet? How big is it next to Earth, do you think?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Why do scientists send machines, not people, this far from home?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘What connects a mountaineer and a spacecraft? Find two things they have in common.’
Lift-off
  1. Question 1
    ‘What do you think this rocket is carrying, and where is it going?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘How would you feel standing a few kilometres away at the moment it takes off?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Have you ever watched a launch, live or online? Which part did you find most exciting?’
A record beside a spacecraft
  1. Question 1
    ‘Read the label. Whose sounds do you think are on this record?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Why would anyone fix a record to a spacecraft instead of a book or a letter?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Records, cassettes, CDs, memory sticks: which of these does your family still keep at home?’
Drawings on a gold cover
  1. Question 1
    ‘What do you think these lines and circles are trying to explain?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Why might the makers have used drawings here and no words at all?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘If you had to explain your life without words, which three pictures would you draw?’
Home, seen from space
  1. Question 1
    ‘Where was the camera when this picture was taken, do you think?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Which parts of the planet can you recognise: oceans, clouds, ice or land?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Would you go into space as a flight doctor? What would worry you most?’
A heartbeat for the stars
  1. Question 1
    ‘Which organ is this, and which of the vessels around it can you name?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘The sound of a human heart went into space on the Golden Record. Why do you think the team chose it for other life forms?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘If you could add one sound from a hospital to that message, which would you choose, and why?’

Lead-in 2 · Life stories, risks and messages — agree or disagree?

4:00Choose a side first, then give one reason and one real example.

1 · You can learn more from a person’s life story than from a textbook.

Model answer

I agree, at least when it comes to remembering things. I’ve forgotten most of the dates in my history textbook, but I still remember my grandfather’s story about carrying wounded soldiers across a river at night. A real person’s choices stay with you much longer than a list of facts.

2 · A famous person’s childhood explains most of their success.

Model answer

I don’t think so. Plenty of people have a happy, comfortable childhood and never do anything special, and one of the best surgeons on my placement grew up selling vegetables at a market. Childhood can open a door, but it’s the hard work in your twenties that gets you through it.

3 · Climbing the world’s highest mountains is worth the risk.

Model answer

Not for me. On our field exercise last spring we only climbed about 1,500 metres, and two cadets still twisted their ankles and had to be helped down. I admire people like Messner, but I’d rather keep all ten toes.

4 · A message for other life forms should contain music, not words.

Model answer

Mostly, yes. Nobody out there will understand Vietnamese or English, but a rhythm might make sense to any creature that can hear. I’d still add one short spoken greeting, though, just to show them we can talk.

5 · Every school should teach the history of space exploration.

Model answer

Not every school, no. Our secondary school timetable was already packed, and I’d rather have had more first aid classes. A couple of lessons as part of physics would be enough, like the afternoon our teacher played the Moon landing on an old projector.

6 · Our phones keep a better record of our lives than any diary.

Model answer

I disagree. My phone has about eight thousand photos, but they show where I was, not what I was thinking. My mum has kept a diary since her first job on a children’s ward, and a single page of it tells you more than a whole album.

Useful language
  • I’m with you on that, because …
  • That’s true for …, but not for …
  • Speaking from my own training, …
  • I’d go along with that, as long as …
  • I’m not so sure about that, because …

Lead-in 3 · What goes into a biography?

6:00Brainstorm first, then put the seven cards in order together.

SB p. 137 Ex 1 · Think of three pieces of information you would expect to find in a biography. Note them below and compare with a partner.

Your three ideas
Model answer
  • Birth date and place
  • Major achievements
  • Career highlights
  • Also common: childhood and family, a turning point, the person’s own words, other people’s opinions, life today or legacy
Lead-in 3

Seven cards about Neil Armstrong: number them 1–7 in the order a biography tells them

Hint: a biography does not always start with the birth.
After flying 78 combat missions for the US Navy in Korea, he became a test pilot, and in 1962 NASA chose him as an astronaut.
Today the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in his hometown tells his story; it opened exactly three years after the Moon landing.
He was born on 5 August 1930 near Wapakoneta, a small town in Ohio, in the United States.
In July 1969, as he stepped down from Apollo 11’s landing craft onto the Moon, he said, ‘That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.’
Neil Armstrong is famous for being the first person to walk on the Moon.
‘Neil was among the greatest of American heroes,’ said President Barack Obama when Armstrong died in 2012.
As a small boy, he went on his first plane ride with his father, and he got a student pilot’s licence on his sixteenth birthday, before he could even drive a car.
The biography in order · clue words highlighted

1Neil Armstrong is famous for being the first person to walk on the Moon.

1 · Why he is well known (topic c). Like paragraph 1 of the Messner text, the opening gives the reason for the person’s fame, not the birth. Only card E names him in full; card C starts with He, so it cannot open the text.

2He was born on 5 August 1930 near Wapakoneta, a small town in Ohio, in the United States.

2 · When and where he was born (topic a). The life story itself starts here: the first item in the model list above.

3As a small boy, he went on his first plane ride with his father, and he got a student pilot’s licence on his sixteenth birthday, before he could even drive a car.

3 · Childhood and early life (topic b). Messner’s father took him up a mountain; Armstrong’s father took him up in a plane.

4After flying 78 combat missions for the US Navy in Korea, he became a test pilot, and in 1962 NASA chose him as an astronaut.

4 · Career highlights. The adult steps that led to his greatest moment, told in time order.

5In July 1969, as he stepped down from Apollo 11’s landing craft onto the Moon, he said, ‘That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.’

5 · The major achievement and something he said (topic d). A comma comes before the opening quotation mark; the full stop sits inside the closing one.

6‘Neil was among the greatest of American heroes,’ said President Barack Obama when Armstrong died in 2012.

6 · What other people have said (topic e). Kammerlander’s words do this job in paragraph 3; here the reporting clause follows the quote.

7Today the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in his hometown tells his story; it opened exactly three years after the Moon landing.

7 · The present: what remains of his life (topic f). The text ends in the present, just as paragraph 4 ends with the Messner Mountain Museum.

Roadmap

Learning outcomes

Reading · SB p. 137 + PET Parts 2–4
  • The world’s greatest mountaineer (listen and read) and 3 PET texts
  • Paragraph topics, reference, inference, the writer’s attitude and purpose
  • At least 70% of the answers right
Listening & viewing · Videos 11.1–11.2 + PET Parts 1, 3, 4
  • Video A: the Golden Record in two parts · Video B: words in context
  • PET: 7 short extracts, a guide’s talk at a space exhibition, a radio interview
  • Numbers, dates, the order of the sounds, who says what
  • 7 or more right in every 10
Speaking · Parts 1–3
  • Part 1: Point → Why → Example, with a chunk from Sheet 4
  • Part 2: 2 minutes on cue card A (Topic 9, a documentary) or B (Topic 4, a historical event)
  • Part 3: the full 7-step frame in roughly a minute
  • Sheet 11: someone’s life in 20 seconds, quoting their own words
Writing · the advantages–disadvantages paragraph
  • One paragraph of 140–170 words, 8–10 sentences
  • A topic sentence that names the side: advantages, disadvantages or both
  • Each point explained and backed by one specific example
  • For both sides: a turning sentence, then a last sentence that weighs them up
Grammar
  • Direct speech: quotation marks, commas, full stops and capitals in the right place
  • Tenses in a life story: finished events, a life that goes on, and today
  • Exercises 7–15: at least 80% correct
Vocabulary
  • Chunks from all 4 groups in your answers and your paragraph
  • Sheet 10 quiz one week later: 13 of the 16 chunks or more
  • Exercises 1–6: at least 80% correct

How to learn a group of words

1

Read the Core aloud

  • Mark the stress: mountainEER, aCHIEVEment, interSTELlar
  • Say every example sentence aloud one time
2

Pick 5 Advanced chunks

  • Choose the five you would use in a life story or a talk about space
  • Save the rest for next week
3

Cover and recall

  • Cover the meaning line: say what the word means in English
  • Cover the headword: find it again from the meaning
4

Write one true sentence

  • About a climb, a trip or a person you admire
  • Use 2 new chunks and the right life-story tense
5

Say it in 30 seconds

  • Your sentence plus two more, with one quote in direct speech
  • Open with Let me tell you about …
Sheet 3 / 11 · 4 vocabulary groups · The greatest mountaineer & the Golden Record

Vocabulary: life stories, high mountains, space and messages

Group 1 · Life stories — writing a biography

Core
A life
be born /bi ˈbɔːn/
come into the world at the start of your life (in a story: was / were …)
My grandmother was born in a mining town in Thái Nguyên, the youngest of nine children.
childhood /ˈtʃaɪldhʊd/
the part of your life between birth and about the age of twelve
Captain Hà spent most of her childhood in a border town, where her father ran the only clinic.
early life /ˌɜːli ˈlaɪf/
the first part of someone's story, from birth until they become an adult
The first chapter covers the surgeon's early life in a poor farming family near the coast.
a teenager /ˈtiːneɪdʒə(r)/
a young person aged between 13 and 19
As a teenager, our new pharmacology lecturer won a national prize for chemistry.
in his / her twenties /ɪn hɪz ˈtwentiz/
aged between 20 and 29
In her twenties, my aunt worked as a nurse on an island off the coast of Quảng Ninh.
grow up /ˌɡrəʊ ˈʌp/
change from a child into an adult; spend your young years in a place
I grew up in the Central Highlands, so steep roads and cold mornings feel normal to me.
die (in an accident) /daɪ/ · /ˈæksɪdənt/
stop living because of something sudden and unplanned, e.g. a fall or a crash
Two farmers died in an accident on the mountain road when a lorry lost its brakes.
retire /rɪˈtaɪə(r)/
stop working, usually because you have reached a certain age
Colonel Minh retired from the army hospital at sixty but still teaches first aid to schoolchildren.
Fame and success
be famous for (+ -ing) /ˈfeɪməs fə(r)/
be known by very many people because of something you did or do
The old field surgeon was famous for operating quickly and calmly, even during air raids.
well-known /ˌwel ˈnəʊn/
recognised by a lot of people
Her father is a well-known heart specialist in Hải Phòng.
a legend /ˈledʒənd/
someone so great in a field that people admire and respect them for years
At our academy, the professor who wrote the first handbook of war surgery is still a legend.
an achievement /əˈtʃiːvmənt/
something important that you manage to do after a lot of effort
Passing the final anatomy exam at the first attempt was a real achievement for our whole class.
achieve /əˈtʃiːv/
succeed in doing something difficult through hard work
After six months of daily training, Quân achieved his goal of running a marathon in under four hours.
admire /ədˈmaɪə(r)/
respect and like someone because of what they are or what they do
I admire the nurses on night duty: they stay calm when everyone else is exhausted.
be described as /dɪˈskraɪbd əz/
be called a certain thing by people who talk or write about you
The new field hospital is often described as a model for the whole region.
a technique /tekˈniːk/
a special way of doing something that you have to learn and practise
In the skills lab, we practised a new technique for stopping heavy bleeding from the thigh.
Advanced
A life that changes things
a pioneer/ˌpaɪəˈnɪə(r)/one of the first people to do something new, who opens the way for othersShe was a pioneer of mountain rescue medicine, and many later teams copied her methods.
a career/kəˈrɪə(r)/the series of jobs someone does during their working lifeUncle Tâm began his career as a medic on a navy ship and ended it as a hospital director.
a turning point/ˈtɜːnɪŋ pɔɪnt/a moment when an important change happens in someone's lifeA summer at a highland clinic was the turning point that made Linh choose emergency medicine.
inspire/ɪnˈspaɪə(r)/give someone the wish and the energy to do somethingStories of army doctors who worked under fire inspired me to apply to the academy.
a legacy/ˈleɡəsi/something good that a person leaves behind after they die or stop workingThe professor's real legacy is not his books but the hundreds of surgeons he trained.
go on to (do)/ˌɡəʊ ˈɒn tə/do something later, after finishing something elseAfter two years as a trekking guide, Duy went on to study nursing in Hanoi.
Collocations
Famous lives
the first man / woman to …/ðə ˌfɜːst ˈmæn tə/the person who did something before anyone elseMai was the first woman in her family to join the army.
set a record/ˌset ə ˈrekɔːd/do something better, faster or more than anyone beforeOur relay team set a new academy record at the spring sports festival.
change the history of …/ˈtʃeɪndʒ ðə ˈhɪstri əv/make a big difference to the way something develops from then onThe first X-ray machines changed the history of medicine: doctors could see a broken bone without cutting the skin.
in history/ɪn ˈhɪstri/of all the times in the past (often after the best, the worst, the first)That was the worst storm in the island's history, and the clinic had to move its patients upstairs.
lose (six toes)/luːz/ · /təʊz/no longer have part of your body after an injury or illnessWithout dry socks, a soldier on a winter patrol can lose his toes to frostbite.
spend more time with/ˌspend ˌmɔː ˈtaɪm wɪð/be together with someone for longer than beforeAfter his last posting abroad, Major Phong asked for a desk job so he could spend more time with his children.

Group 2 · Mountains and adventure — climbing and its risks

Core
Climbing
a mountaineer /ˌmaʊntəˈnɪə(r)/
a person who goes up very high peaks as a sport or a job
The mountaineers waited three days in their tents for the wind to drop.
a climber /ˈklaɪmə(r)/
someone who tackles rock faces, indoor walls or peaks for sport
Our academy's best climber can get to the top of the indoor wall in under a minute.
climb (up) /klaɪm/
go up something steep, using your hands and feet
We climbed up the steep path to the radar station with twenty-kilo packs on our backs.
a mountain /ˈmaʊntən/
a very high hill, often with rock or snow at the top
Fansipan is the highest mountain in Vietnam, at just over 3,100 metres.
the summit /ˈsʌmɪt/
the highest point of a peak
Thick cloud hid the summit all morning, and we only saw it at sunset.
oxygen /ˈɒksɪdʒən/
the gas in the air that people and animals need to breathe
Patients with a serious lung infection often need extra oxygen through a mask.
an accident /ˈæksɪdənt/
a bad event that happens by chance and often hurts someone
After the accident on the assault course, one cadet needed six stitches in his chin.
dangerous /ˈdeɪndʒərəs/
likely to hurt or kill someone
Crossing a river in flood is dangerous, even for strong swimmers.
a risk /rɪsk/
the chance that something bad will happen
Sleeping in wet clothes on a cold night carries a real risk of hypothermia.
the Himalayas /ðə ˌhɪməˈleɪəz/
the highest range of peaks on Earth, in South Asia, with Everest among them
Many young doctors dream of joining a trek in the Himalayas to see how the body copes with thin air.
Places and people
a village /ˈvɪlɪdʒ/
a very small town in the countryside
The medical team set up a tent clinic in a village two hours' walk from the nearest road.
a valley /ˈvæli/
the low land between two lines of hills, often with a river
From the pass, we could see the whole valley below us, bright green with young rice.
a rock /rɒk/
a large, hard piece of stone
The guide sat on a flat rock and checked everyone's feet for blisters.
a team /tiːm/
a group of people who work or play together
Each rescue team has a doctor, a nurse and two stretcher-bearers.
a guide /ɡaɪd/
a person whose job is to show others the way and keep them safe
Our local guide knew which paths were too slippery after the rain.
Advanced
Higher and harder
an expedition/ˌekspəˈdɪʃn/a long, organised journey by a group to a distant or difficult placeThe army sent a small medical expedition to the islands to check the children's health.
altitude/ˈæltɪtjuːd/the height of a place above the level of the seaAt high altitude, water boils at a lower temperature, so rice takes longer to cook.
altitude sickness/ˈæltɪtjuːd ˌsɪknəs/an illness with headache, nausea and tiredness that people get when they go up too high, too fastOn the third day of the trek, two cadets had headaches and no appetite: classic signs of altitude sickness.
a peak/piːk/the pointed top of a mountain, or the mountain itselfSnow covers the highest peaks even in the hottest months of the year.
reach the top/ˌriːtʃ ðə ˈtɒp/get to the highest pointIt took us five hours to reach the top of the hill and only two to come down.
extreme/ɪkˈstriːm/very great, much more than usual; or very dangerousSoldiers on border duty in winter must cope with extreme cold and long, dark nights.
Collocations
On the mountain
without oxygen/wɪˌðaʊt ˈɒksɪdʒən/with no bottled gas to help you breatheDoctors still study how a climber's body copes at such heights without oxygen from a tank.
over eight thousand metres/ˌəʊvər ˌeɪt ˈθaʊznd ˈmiːtəz/higher than 8,000 m above sea levelThe air at over eight thousand metres is so thin that climbers call it ‘the death zone’.
take a risk/ˌteɪk ə ˈrɪsk/do something although you know that something bad might happenGood rescue leaders don't take risks with the weather; they wait for a clear day.
a dangerous climb/ˌdeɪndʒərəs ˈklaɪm/a difficult way up where people could get hurtThe final stretch of the route is a dangerous climb over loose stones and ice.
reach the summit/ˌriːtʃ ðə ˈsʌmɪt/get to the very top of the peakOnly four of the eleven climbers reached the summit; the others turned back because of the wind.
a mountain museum/ˌmaʊntən mjuˈziːəm/a place that shows objects and stories about high places and the people who go up themOur guide's tiny mountain museum is full of old ropes, boots and photos of the first climbs in the area.

Group 3 · Space exploration — spacecraft, planets and missions

Core
Space
space /speɪs/
the area beyond the Earth's air, where the planets and stars are
From space, astronauts can see the lights of big cities at night.
a spacecraft /ˈspeɪskrɑːft/
a machine built to travel beyond the Earth's air, with or without people on board
The spacecraft carries cameras, radios and a power source that should last for years.
launch /lɔːntʃ/
send a rocket up into the sky; also, start something new
We watched the engineers launch the rocket on a live video, and the whole lecture hall went silent.
the solar system /ðə ˈsəʊlə sɪstəm/
the Sun and all the planets and other objects that move round it
Of all the planets in the solar system, only Earth is known to have life.
a planet /ˈplænɪt/
a large round object in space that moves round a star
Mars is called the red planet because of the iron-rich dust on its surface.
the universe /ðə ˈjuːnɪvɜːs/
all of space and everything that exists in it
When you see how many galaxies there are in the universe, your exam worries suddenly seem very small.
a star /stɑː(r)/
a huge ball of burning gas that we see as a point of light at night
On the field exercise in the hills, there were so many stars that the sky looked almost white.
Earth /ɜːθ/
the world we live on, the third planet from the Sun
Seen from the Moon, Earth looks like a small blue and white ball.
a mission /ˈmɪʃn/
an important job that a person or a group is sent to do
The medical team's mission was to vaccinate every child on the island in one week.
a function /ˈfʌŋkʃn/
the purpose or job that something has
The main function of the kidneys is to clean the blood.
People and science
a scientist /ˈsaɪəntɪst/
an expert who studies the natural world through careful experiments
The scientists in the lab work in pairs, so one can check the other's results.
an astronaut /ˈæstrənɔːt/
a person trained to travel and work in a spacecraft
Astronauts on the space station exercise for about two hours a day to keep their bones and muscles strong.
a satellite /ˈsætəlaɪt/
a machine sent up to go round the Earth and collect or pass on information
The map on your phone uses satellites to show exactly where you are.
explore /ɪkˈsplɔː(r)/
travel round a place to learn about it
On our last day in Đà Lạt, we hired bikes and explored the pine forests around the lake.
exploration /ˌekspləˈreɪʃn/
the act of travelling to unknown places to find out about them
The exploration of the caves in Quảng Bình has shown how much of our own country we still don't know.
discover /dɪˈskʌvə(r)/
find something, or learn a fact, for the first time
Doctors discovered that the patient's chest pain came from a broken rib, not his heart.
Advanced
Deep space
interstellar/ˌɪntəˈstelə(r)/between the stars; in the area beyond our Sun's reachA message drifting through interstellar space may travel for thousands of years before anything finds it.
an orbit/ˈɔːbɪt/the curved path of an object as it travels round a planet, moon or starThe space station completes an orbit of the Earth about every ninety minutes.
a probe/prəʊb/a spacecraft with no people on board, sent to collect informationThe probe sent back the first close-up pictures of the planet's icy rings.
life forms/ˈlaɪf fɔːmz/living things of any kind, especially ones we do not know yetSome scientists think tiny life forms could exist in the ocean under the ice of one of Jupiter's moons.
a space agency/ˈspeɪs eɪdʒənsi/a government organisation that plans and runs flights beyond the EarthNASA is the American space agency, and it shares most of its photos with the public for free.
data/ˈdeɪtə/facts and numbers collected for studyThe nurse entered each patient's data into the computer before the ward round.
Collocations
A spacecraft's journey
be launched into space/lɔːntʃt ˌɪntə ˈspeɪs/be sent up from the Earth on a rocketVietnam's first telecommunications satellite, VINASAT-1, was launched into space in April 2008.
fly past a planet/ˌflaɪ ˌpɑːst ə ˈplænɪt/travel close to a world in space without stopping or landingA probe that flies past a planet has only a few hours to take its best pictures.
send back photographs/ˌsend ˈbæk ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːfs/return pictures to the place you came fromThe rover on Mars sends back photographs that help scientists choose where to drive it next.
complete a mission/kəmˌpliːt ə ˈmɪʃn/finish the job you were sent to doThe helicopter crew completed their mission and brought all three injured fishermen back to shore.
further into space/ˌfɜːðər ˌɪntə ˈspeɪs/a greater distance away from the EarthEngineers are designing engines that could carry crews further into space, perhaps as far as Mars.
leave the solar system/ˌliːv ðə ˈsəʊlə sɪstəm/go beyond the whole region ruled by the Sun's gravity, past the far edge of the Oort CloudVoyager 1 is already in interstellar space, but it will need about 30,000 more years to leave the solar system completely.

Group 4 · Messages and records — a message for other worlds

Core
Recording
a record /ˈrekɔːd/
a flat round disc that holds sound and is played on a special machine
My grandfather still plays his old records of wartime songs every Sunday morning.
record (v) /rɪˈkɔːd/
store sounds or pictures so that people can hear or see them later
Please don't record the lecture without asking the professor first.
a recording /rɪˈkɔːdɪŋ/
a piece of sound or film that has been stored
We listened to a recording of a patient's heartbeat and tried to find the extra sound.
a message /ˈmesɪdʒ/
a short piece of information that you send or leave for someone
I left a message with the duty officer, saying I would be back by nine.
a greeting /ˈɡriːtɪŋ/
words or a sign that you use to say hello or welcome someone
The guide taught us a short greeting in the H'Mông language before we entered the village.
a voice /vɔɪs/
the sound you make when you speak or sing
The patient's voice was weak, so I had to sit close to the bed to hear her.
a language /ˈlæŋɡwɪdʒ/
the system of words that the people of a country or group use
Vietnam has more than fifty ethnic groups, and many of them have their own language.
represent /ˌreprɪˈzent/
stand for something, or speak and act for a group
Three cadets will represent our academy at the national first-aid competition.
fix (onto) · attach /fɪks/ · /əˈtætʃ/
fasten one thing firmly to another
We fixed a name tag onto each stretcher and attached a torch to the handle.
Music and memory
classical music /ˌklæsɪkl ˈmjuːzɪk/
serious European pieces in the style of Bach or Mozart, often played by an orchestra
Some surgeons play classical music during long operations because it helps them focus.
jazz /dʒæz/
a kind of music with strong rhythms, first played by African American musicians in New Orleans
A small band plays jazz in a café near the lake every Friday night.
traditional music /trəˌdɪʃənl ˈmjuːzɪk/
old songs and tunes that a culture has passed down for generations
Quan họ singing is the traditional music of Bắc Ninh, and UNESCO lists it as intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
a memory stick /ˈmeməri stɪk/
a small device that you plug into a computer to store files
I saved my presentation on a memory stick in case the lecture-hall computer didn't work.
digital /ˈdɪdʒɪtl/
using computers and numbers to store information, not paper or film
All patient notes at the new hospital are digital, so doctors can read them from any ward.
someday /ˈsʌmdeɪ/
at a time in the future that is not known yet
Someday I'd like to work as a doctor on a research ship in Antarctica.
Advanced
Messages for the future
symbolise/ˈsɪmbəlaɪz/be a sign of an idea or a qualityIn many cultures, a white dove symbolises peace.
a time capsule/ˈtaɪm kæpsjuːl/a box of objects and letters kept for people in the future to openOur class put photos and letters in a time capsule, to be opened at our twentieth reunion.
preserve/prɪˈzɜːv/keep something in its original state so that it is not lost or damagedThe library scans old medical journals to preserve them before the paper falls apart.
a reply/rɪˈplaɪ/an answer to a letter, a call or a messageI emailed the course director on Monday, but I still haven't had a reply.
on behalf of/ɒn bɪˈhɑːf əv/for someone else, or as their representativeThe class monitor accepted the prize on behalf of the whole class.
a generation/ˌdʒenəˈreɪʃn/all the people born at about the same timeMy grandparents' generation lived most of their lives without phones or the internet.

send a message into space/ˌsend ə ˈmesɪdʒ ˌɪntə ˈspeɪs/use radio signals or a spacecraft to carry words beyond the EarthIn 1974, scientists sent a radio message into space from a huge telescope in Puerto Rico.
represent different parts of the world/ˌreprɪˈzent/stand for many regions and cultures of the globeThe flags in the hall represent different parts of the world where our army doctors have served.

lots of digital memory/ˌlɒts əv ˌdɪdʒɪtl ˈmeməri/a large amount of storage space on a computer or deviceVideos of surgery take up lots of digital memory, so the department bought a bigger server.
send a reply/ˌsend ə rɪˈplaɪ/answer a messagePlease send a reply by Friday so that we know how many seats to book on the bus.

VerbUse it when …Shape

10 functions · 30 chunks

1 · Saying when and where someone was born

  • … was born in (year) in (place).
  • … was born on (date), the … of … children.
  • … comes from …, a small … in the north of …

Sergeant Tuấn comes from Mộc Châu, a small town on a tea-growing plateau in the north of Vietnam.

2 · Saying why someone is famous

  • … is famous for + -ing …
  • … is best known for …
  • … was the first … to …

Our anatomy professor is best known for his hand-drawn diagrams of the heart.

3 · Talking about childhood and early life

  • As a child, …
  • When … was only …, …
  • … grew up in …, where …

When she was only twelve, she looked after her sick grandmother every night.

4 · Talking about a difficult moment and what came next

  • In …, things went badly wrong: …
  • …; nevertheless, … carried on …
  • That was the turning point: from then on, …

He failed the fitness test twice; nevertheless, he carried on training and passed with top marks a year later.

5 · Quoting someone's words

  • As … once said, ‘…’
  • ‘…,’ says …
  • In an interview, … told reporters, ‘…’

As our first commander once said, ‘A medic's hands must move faster than his fear.’

6 · Saying what other people think of someone

  • … has been described as …
  • Many people regard … as …
  • … is widely seen as …

Many cadets regard Professor Bình as the best teacher they have ever had.

7 · Saying what someone does now · their legacy

  • Nowadays, … spends most of his / her time …
  • Today, … still …
  • … will be remembered for …

Nowadays, she spends most of her time training young paramedics in the highlands.

8 · Introducing an advantage

  • One clear advantage of + -ing … is that …
  • The main benefit of … is …
  • Another plus is that …

One clear advantage of teaching first aid at school is that children know what to do before the ambulance arrives.

9 · Introducing a disadvantage

  • The main drawback of … is that …
  • On the downside, …
  • A serious problem with … is that …

The main drawback of online lectures is that you can't ask the lecturer a quick question.

10 · Weighing up and concluding

  • On balance, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages because …
  • Overall, …, as long as …
  • Although …, I believe the benefits are greater because …

Overall, a winter training camp in the hills pays off, as long as a doctor goes with every group.

From B1 to B1+ / B2: 12 upgrade pairs

B1B1+ / B2
His parents were poor farmers. He was born in 1950.The son of poor rice farmers, he was born in 1950 and walked five kilometres to school every morning as a teenager.
She is famous because she led a team.She is best known for leading the first all-female rescue team in the province.
Many people like this surgeon.He has been described as one of the most admired surgeons of his generation.
He had an accident, but he continued.He badly hurt his back in a climbing accident; nevertheless, he went on to become a spine surgeon.
She said the valley was beautiful.‘I've never seen anything so beautiful,’ she whispered, looking down at the valley.
Now he writes books.Nowadays he spends more time at home, and he has written three books about his years as an army doctor.
The rocket went into space.The rocket was launched into space just after sunrise and reached orbit about nine minutes later.
The spacecraft is very far away now.The probe is now so far away that its radio signals take almost a whole day to reach Earth.
We will put songs on the memory stick.We'd include a quan họ duet, a jazz standard and a Bach cello suite to represent three very different cultures.
It is a message for aliens.It is a recorded message for any life forms that might find it someday.
Climbing very high is dangerous.Climbers take huge risks at extreme altitude, where one wrong step can be fatal.
Mountain trips are good and bad.Training trips to the mountains have real advantages; on the downside, they are cold, costly and sometimes risky.

The answer frame — 7 steps

Sample question: ‘Is it better to learn about a famous person from a biography or from a documentary?’

1Point

State your choice clearly in the very first sentence.

If you ask me, …

2Why

Give the one reason that matters most to you.

That's mainly because …

3How

Show how that reason works in real life.

When you …, you …

4Example

Tell one real case: a book, a film, a day you remember.

I remember …

5Result

Say what happened because of that one case.

As a result, …

6Limitation

Admit what the other side does better.

Admittedly, …

7Evaluation

Weigh both sides and end on a new angle, not the Point again.

All in all, …

Model answer · all seven steps in a single paragraph

In the model answers: Point = step of the answer frame · frame language = opinion, reason, example, contrast, conclusion · unit vocabulary = a word or phrase from the four Sheet 3 groups

PointIf you ask me, a good biography teaches you more about a famous person than a documentary does. WhyThat's mainly because a book has room for the small, private details of someone's childhood and career that a ninety-minute film usually cuts. HowWhen you read, you can stop, go back a page and think about why someone made a choice, and you often hear their own words in the letters and diaries the writer quotes. ExampleI remember reading a biography of Marie Curie in my first year. The part that stayed with me came from a private diary she kept after her husband Pierre was killed in a street accident in 1906: she went on writing to him as if he could still read it, telling him about the spring flowers he would have liked. I've never seen that in any film about her. ResultAs a result, she stopped being a name from our physics lectures and became a real person to me, and I finished the whole book in four days. LimitationAdmittedly, a documentary is quicker, and it can take you inside the lab in Paris where she worked, which is now a small museum. EvaluationAll in all, the best order is probably film first, book second: the film makes you curious in one evening, and the book keeps you thinking for weeks.

Where to use it
  • Speaking Part 1: only Point → Why → Example, in roughly thirty seconds.
  • Speaking Part 2: share the seven steps out among the cue-card prompts and keep the Evaluation for the final ‘and explain why …’ line.
  • Speaking Part 3: all seven steps, about one short sentence each, for close to a minute.
  • Advantages–disadvantages paragraph (Sheet 8): Point = your opening line, saying which side(s) you will cover · Why/How + Example = one benefit or drawback with its own case · Limitation = the turn (However, … / On the other hand, …) · Evaluation = a closing weigh-up with nothing new in it.

12 common mistakes

MistakeCorrectionRemember
The sergeant said ‘Lights out at ten’.The sergeant said, ‘Lights out at ten.’said needs a comma; the final full stop belongs to the quote.
‘We're lost.’ she whispered.‘We're lost,’ she whispered.when she whispered follows, the quote closes with a comma.
‘Is it far,’ asked the cadet?‘Is it far?’ asked the cadet.the question mark belongs to the words spoken, so it goes inside.
‘Don't move,’ said he.‘Don't move,’ he said.with he / she / they, the verb comes second: he said, she asked.
She born in a village near the Lao border.She was born in a village near the Lao border.be born always needs was / were for a past birth.
My grandfather was born on 1952.My grandfather was born in 1952.in + a year · on + a full date.
He has joined the army in 2010.He joined the army in 2010.a finished time (in 2010) → past simple.
The village doctor is famous for help women give birth safely.The village doctor is famous for helping women give birth safely.a preposition (for) + verb-ing.
She was the first nurse in the province reached the summit.She was the first nurse in the province to reach the summit.after first, only, youngest → to + verb, not a past tense.
The advantage of live near the hospital is a short trip to work.The advantage of living near the hospital is a short trip to work.the advantage of + verb-ing or a noun.
An advantage is can save a lot of money.An advantage is that it saves a lot of money.is that + a full clause with its own subject.
In my view, the benefits are outweigh the costs.In my view, the benefits outweigh the costs.outweigh is a verb: no are before it.

Passage | Questions
Played 0×

The world's greatest mountaineer.

Reinhold Messner has been described as the greatest mountaineer in history. He's famous for being one of the first men to climb Mount Everest without oxygen in 1978. But he was also the first man to climb all fourteen of the world's mountains over eight thousand metres.

Messner was born in 1944 in a small village in the mountains of northern Italy. When he talks about the area he still says, ‘it's the most beautiful place in the world.’ His father was a climber and took his son up a mountain when he was only five. As a teenager, Messner climbed with his younger brother Günther.

In their twenties, the two brothers started climbing in the Himalayas, but Günther died in an accident and Reinhold lost six toes. Nevertheless, Reinhold continued climbing and he became a legend among other mountaineers. The climber Hans Kammerlander believes Reinhold changed climbing. ‘Reinhold had so many new ideas,’ says Kammerlander. ‘He found new ways, new techniques.’

Nowadays Messner spends more time at home with his family and he has written over sixty books. In 2006 he opened the first Messner Mountain Museum, where people can find out more about the world he loves.

The world's greatest mountaineer

1What is the main job of paragraph 1?
1What is the main job of paragraph 1?
Each of its three sentences gives a reason for his fame: ‘has been described as the greatest mountaineer in history’, ‘one of the first men to climb Mount Everest without oxygen’, ‘the first man to climb all fourteen …’. The village and his childhood only start in paragraph 2, and no climb is told day by day.Clue: SB Ex 2 topic c: why he became well-known. Read paragraph 1 as a whole.
In the text: Reinhold Messner has been described as the greatest mountaineer in history. He's famous for being one of the first men to climb Mount Everest without oxygen in 1978. But he was also the first man to climb all fourteen of the world's mountains over eight thousand metres.
2Reinhold Messner has been described as the greatest mountaineer in history. This means that …
2Reinhold Messner has been described as the greatest mountaineer in history. This means that …
The passive hides who said it, because many people have said it over many years. It is not Messner's own claim, the writer does not try to prove it, and the present perfect (has been) shows it is still said today, not only in the past.Clue: TB note: has been described as = people have said that he is …
In the text: Reinhold Messner has been described as the greatest mountaineer in history.
3He's famous for being one of the first men to climb Mount Everest without oxygen. What can we infer?
3He's famous for being one of the first men to climb Mount Everest without oxygen. What can we infer?
If he was one of the first, at least one other climber did it at about the same time. (In fact he reached the top with the Austrian climber Peter Habeler on 8 May 1978.) Everest had been climbed before 1978, but with oxygen.Clue: one of the first = one person in a small group who were first.
In the text: He's famous for being one of the first men to climb Mount Everest without oxygen in 1978.
4SB Exercise 2 (a birth · b childhood · c fame · d his own words · e others' opinions · f now): which three topics are all in paragraph 2?
4SB Exercise 2 (a birth · b childhood · c fame · d his own words · e others' opinions · f now): which three topics are all in paragraph 2?
Born ‘in 1944 in a small village in the mountains of northern Italy’ (a); a mountain at five, climbing with Günther as a teenager (b); ‘he still says, “it's the most beautiful place in the world.”’ (d). Other people's opinions (e) come in paragraph 3, today (f) in paragraph 4, his fame (c) in paragraph 1.Clue: SB Ex 2 key: a → 2 · b → 2 · c → 1 · d → 2 · e → 3 · f → 4.
In the text: Messner was born in 1944 in a small village in the mountains of northern Italy. When he talks about the area he still says, “it's the most beautiful place in the world.” His father was a climber and took his son up a mountain when he was only five. As a teenager, Messner climbed with his younger brother Günther.
5Paragraph 2: what does it refer to in he still says, ‘it's the most beautiful place in the world’?
5Paragraph 2: what does it refer to in he still says, ‘it's the most beautiful place in the world’?
‘When he talks about the area he still says, “it's the most beautiful place …”’ The area is the place in the mountains of northern Italy where his village is, named in the sentence before. Everest and the Himalayas only appear later; the museum is in paragraph 4.Clue: Reference: it points back to a noun earlier in the same sentence.
In the text: Messner was born in 1944 in a small village in the mountains of northern Italy. When he talks about the area he still says, “it's the most beautiful place in the world.”
6Nevertheless, Reinhold continued climbing. What does Nevertheless tell the reader?
6Nevertheless, Reinhold continued climbing. What does Nevertheless tell the reader?
First the bad news: ‘Günther died in an accident and Reinhold lost six toes.’ Then Nevertheless: he did what we would not expect and ‘continued climbing’. The word shows contrast; it gives no reason, and nothing says he stopped or went to look for his brother.Clue: Nevertheless = in spite of what has just been said (like however).
In the text: In their twenties, the two brothers started climbing in the Himalayas, but Günther died in an accident and Reinhold lost six toes. Nevertheless, Reinhold continued climbing
7… he became a legend among other mountaineers. Here, a legend is …
7… he became a legend among other mountaineers. Here, a legend is …
among other mountaineers tells us who admires him: people in the same activity. The meaning ‘an old story that may not be true’ does not fit a real, living climber, and the next sentence adds a fellow climber's praise.Clue: TB note: a legend = someone so famous or important in a field that others admire and respect them very much.
In the text: and he became a legend among other mountaineers.
8‘He found new ways, new techniques.’ What are techniques?
8‘He found new ways, new techniques.’ What are techniques?
Kammerlander says the same thing twice in different words: so many new ideas → new ways, new techniques. Messner changed how people climb, which is a skill. Equipment, routes and books are things, not methods.Clue: TB note: techniques = ways of doing something that you have to learn.
In the text: “Reinhold had so many new ideas,” says Kammerlander. “He found new ways, new techniques.”
9SB Exercise 3a: whose words does the biography quote directly, and which quotation is split into two parts by the reporting clause?
9SB Exercise 3a: whose words does the biography quote directly, and which quotation is split into two parts by the reporting clause?
Messner's words follow the reporting clause: ‘he still says, “it's the most beautiful place in the world.”’ Kammerlander's words come in two parts with the reporting clause in the middle: ‘“Reinhold had so many new ideas,” says Kammerlander. “He found new ways, new techniques.”’ (comma inside the first part, full stop after says Kammerlander, new quotation marks). Kammerlander believes Reinhold changed climbing has no quotation marks, and nobody else is quoted. Note: the book starts Messner's quotation with a small letter (‘he still says, “it's …”’), but in your own writing a quotation starts with a capital letter (‘It's …’).Clue: Sheet 4 · Grammar 1: a quotation can be split by the reporting clause (‘…,’ he said. ‘…’).
In the text: When he talks about the area he still says, “it's the most beautiful place in the world.” “Reinhold had so many new ideas,” says Kammerlander. “He found new ways, new techniques.”
10In which paragraph does the writer give a named climber's opinion of Messner, and in which does he say what Messner does nowadays?

Paragraph 3: ‘The climber Hans Kammerlander believes Reinhold changed climbing.’ Paragraph 4 opens with Nowadays: ‘Messner spends more time at home … he has written over sixty books.’ Paragraph 1 reports praise (has been described as) but names nobody.Clue: SB Ex 2 key: e → paragraph 3, f → paragraph 4.

Life stories worth your time

AThe Doctor Who Walked (book) For thirty years, Dr Elena Varga walked to patients in eleven mountain villages, along paths where no car could go. Her daughter tells the story through letters, diaries and family photographs. The short chapters make the book easy to read on a bus or a train, and it ends with Elena's advice to young doctors. Paperback or e-book.

BTen Thousand Hearts (TV series) This two-part series follows the heart surgeon Samuel Adeyemi from his first day at medical school to his final operation forty years later.Q10 Viewers see real operations, filmed with the patients' permission, and colleagues explain how his methods changed their hospital. Watch online, with subtitles in twelve languages, including Vietnamese.Q10

CAlone on the Water (audiobook) At sixty-three, Marta Ruiz sailed alone around the world in a boat only nine metres long. In nine hours of recording, she reads her own storyQ6: storms in the Southern Ocean, a broken mast, and the long nights when she talked to the seabirds. Download it to your phone and listen wherever you are.Q6

DStar Notebook (graphic biography) The life of a young astronomer who discovered a comet at nineteen, told in comic-strip pictures. Each chapter is only ten pages longQ8, and the drawings of the night sky are beautiful. At the back, readers will find simple instructions for finding planets without a telescope. Recommended for ages 12 to 16.Q8

EBack on the Rock (book) After a fall in which he broke both legs, the climber Tom Reyes was told that he would never climb again. Two years later he was back in the mountains.Q7 In this honest book he describes every stage of his recovery, and each chapter ends with exercises from his physiotherapist that readers can try at home.Q7

FThe Sound Collector (documentary film) For forty years, Ingrid Holm travelled the world with a microphone, recording birds, frogs and forests that are now disappearing.Q9 This 75-minute film follows her at work and lets audiences hear some of her rarest recordings. In cinemas from this Friday; groups of five or more pay half price.Q9

Extra practice · PET Reading Part 3 · Junko Tabei: the first woman on top of Everest

Questions 11–15. Read the article about the Japanese climber Junko Tabei and the five questions on it. For each question, choose the right answer.

Passage | Questions

Junko Tabei: the first woman on top of Everest

Junko Tabei was born in 1939 in Miharu, a small town in Fukushima, in the north of Japan. People thought of her as a weak child, and nobody expected her to become a climber. Then, at the age of ten, she went on a school trip to Mount Nasu. She loved the views from the top, and she liked the fact that climbing was not a race: nobody had to beat anybody else to reach the summit.Q11

After university, Tabei joined climbing clubs in which almost every member was a man. Some of the men refused to climb with her, and others believed she was only there to find a husband. So in 1969 she started Japan's first climbing club for women.Q12 The next year, she and another member of the club reached the top of Annapurna III in Nepal.

Everest was a much bigger challenge. The Japanese Women's Everest Expedition of 1975 had fifteen members. Finding sponsors was hard, and some people told the women they should be at home looking after their children. In the end, a newspaper and a TV company agreed to help, but each member still had to pay a large part of the cost herself. Tabei paid her share by giving piano lessonsQ13, and she saved money by making some of her own equipment: her waterproof gloves were cut from the cover of her car.Q13

On 4 May 1975, an avalanche hit the team's camp at 6,300 metres during the night. Tabei and four other climbers were buried under the snow, and Sherpa guides had to dig her out.Q14 She was so badly bruised that she could hardly walk, but she would not go back down. Twelve days later, on 16 May, she reached the summit with the Sherpa Ang TseringQ14 and became the first woman to stand on top of the world.

Fame did not change her plans. In 1992 she became the first woman to climb the ‘Seven Summits’, the highest mountain on each continent. Later, she studied the rubbish that climbers leave on Everest, and after the 2011 earthquake in Japan, she led young people affected by the disaster up Mount Fuji every year, even after she became ill with cancer.Q15 She died in 2016, at the age of 77. ‘I did not intend to be the first woman on Everest,’ she once said. For her, it was one climb in a long life of climbing.Q15

11What did Tabei enjoy about climbing when she was young?
11What did Tabei enjoy about climbing when she was young?
‘climbing was not a race: nobody had to beat anybody else to reach the summit.’ In other words, it was not a competition. The text does say she was seen as a weak child, but it never says climbing made her healthier, and there were no prizes.Clue: Paragraph 1: she liked the fact that …
In the text: People thought of her as a weak child, and nobody expected her to become a climber. Then, at the age of ten, she went on a school trip to Mount Nasu. She loved the views from the top, and she liked the fact that climbing was not a race: nobody had to beat anybody else to reach the summit.
12Why does the writer mention what some men in the climbing clubs believed?
12Why does the writer mention what some men in the climbing clubs believed?
‘Some of the men refused to climb with her, and others believed she was only there to find a husband.’ They did not see her as a real climber, and So shows that this is why she started a club for women. Her husband and her teachers play no part here.Clue: Purpose: why give these details just before So in 1969 …?
In the text: Some of the men refused to climb with her, and others believed she was only there to find a husband. So in 1969 she started Japan's first climbing club for women.
13What does the writer say about paying for the 1975 expedition?
13What does the writer say about paying for the 1975 expedition?
‘a newspaper and a TV company agreed to help, but each member still had to pay a large part of the cost herself. Tabei paid her share by giving piano lessons.’ Her car only gave her material for her gloves; she did not sell it, and the sponsors did not cover everything.Clue: Paragraph 3: each member still had to pay …
In the text: Finding sponsors was hard, and some people told the women they should be at home looking after their children. In the end, a newspaper and a TV company agreed to help, but each member still had to pay a large part of the cost herself. Tabei paid her share by giving piano lessons her waterproof gloves were cut from the cover of her car.
14What happened after the avalanche?
14What happened after the avalanche?
She was ‘so badly bruised that she could hardly walk, but she would not go back down’, and ‘Twelve days later, on 16 May, she reached the summit with the Sherpa Ang Tsering.’ Sherpa guides dug her out, nobody is reported dead, and she did not climb alone.Clue: Paragraph 4: she would not go back down + Twelve days later.
In the text: On 4 May 1975, an avalanche hit the team's camp at 6,300 metres during the night. Tabei and four other climbers were buried under the snow, and Sherpa guides had to dig her out. She was so badly bruised that she could hardly walk, but she would not go back down. Twelve days later, on 16 May, she reached the summit with the Sherpa Ang Tsering
15Which of these would Tabei most probably say about her life?
15Which of these would Tabei most probably say about her life?
After Everest she climbed the Seven Summits, studied the rubbish on Everest and led young people up Mount Fuji until the end of her life, and she said, ‘I did not intend to be the first woman on Everest.’ For her, Everest was one part of a long climbing life; fame and money were never the reason.Clue: Global question: put paragraph 5 and her own words together.
In the text: Fame did not change her plans. In 1992 she became the first woman to climb the “Seven Summits”, the highest mountain on each continent. Later, she studied the rubbish that climbers leave on Everest, and after the 2011 earthquake in Japan, she led young people affected by the disaster up Mount Fuji every year, even after she became ill with cancer. “I did not intend to be the first woman on Everest,” she once said. For her, it was one climb in a long life of climbing.

Extra practice · PET Reading Part 4 · A night at the observatory

Questions 16–20. Five sentences have been removed from the story. For each gap, choose the sentence (A–F) under the text that fits best. One sentence is extra.

Passage | Questions

A night at the observatory

Last spring, the academy's astronomy club went on a field trip to a university observatory in the hills, about three hours north of the city. I had only joined the club to fill my free evenings, and I knew almost nothing about stars. (16) …………… By the time our bus reached the top of the hill, the sky was covered in thick grey cloud, and some of us were already complaining.Q16

The astronomer who met us, Dr Vân, did not seem worried at all. ‘Clouds come and go,’ she said. ‘The sky is patient, so we must be patient too.’Q17,Q20 (17) …………… For the next four hours, over cup after cup, she explained how a telescope works and showed us photographs sent back by spacecraft.Q17

Just after two in the morning, someone shouted from the door.Q18 (18) …………… Within minutes we were all at the telescope, and when my turn came I saw a small yellow ball with a perfect ring around it: Saturn.Q16,Q18 I had seen it a hundred times in books, but it had never looked so real.

Later, Dr Vân pointed out a faint star and told us that its light had left it hundreds of years ago.Q19 (19) …………… That thought stayed with me all the way home.Q19

I still go to the club every month. (20) …………… On night duty at the hospital, when test results are slow to come back and everyone around me is in a hurry, I remember Dr Vân's words about the sky and try to wait calmly.Q20

A ‘So you are not seeing the star as it is now,’ she said, ‘but as it was before any of us were born.’

B Our leader, Captain Hòa, had promised us the clearest sky of the year, but the weather had other ideas.

C Sadly, the clouds never cleared, and we went home without seeing a single star.

D The clouds had gone, and the sky was suddenly full of stars.

E But the most useful thing I learned that night had nothing to do with stars.

F Instead of sending us back to the bus, she took us inside and made us tea.

16Gap 16

C (no stars all night) cannot fit anywhere: later the writer sees Saturn.Clue: After the gap: the sky is covered in thick grey cloud.
In the text: By the time our bus reached the top of the hill, the sky was covered in thick grey cloud, and some of us were already complaining. Within minutes we were all at the telescope, and when my turn came I saw a small yellow ball with a perfect ring around it: Saturn.
17Gap 17
17Gap 17
F: ‘Instead of sending us back to the bus, she took us inside and made us tea.’ It shows that she really was not worried (the sentence before), and it explains the cups and the four hours spent indoors.Clue: After the gap: over cup after cup. Cups of what?
In the text: The astronomer who met us, Dr Vân, did not seem worried at all. “Clouds come and go,” she said. “The sky is patient, so we must be patient too.” For the next four hours, over cup after cup, she explained how a telescope works and showed us photographs sent back by spacecraft.
18Gap 18
18Gap 18
D: ‘The clouds had gone, and the sky was suddenly full of stars.’ That is the news someone shouted from the door, and it explains why they were all at the telescope within minutes. C says the opposite.Clue: Before the gap: someone shouts; after it: everyone hurries to the telescope.
In the text: Just after two in the morning, someone shouted from the door. Within minutes we were all at the telescope, and when my turn came I saw a small yellow ball with a perfect ring around it: Saturn.
19Gap 19
19Gap 19
A: ‘So you are not seeing the star as it is now,’ she said, ‘but as it was before any of us were born.’ It explains what ‘its light had left it hundreds of years ago’ means for the person looking, and That thought points back to it.Clue: After the gap: That thought stayed with me. Which sentence is a thought?
In the text: Later, Dr Vân pointed out a faint star and told us that its light had left it hundreds of years ago. That thought stayed with me all the way home.
20Gap 20
20Gap 20
E: ‘But the most useful thing I learned that night had nothing to do with stars.’ But contrasts with going to the star club every month, and the next sentence names the useful thing: waiting calmly, as in ‘The sky is patient, so we must be patient too.’Clue: After the gap: night duty at the hospital and Dr Vân's words.
In the text: The astronomer who met us, Dr Vân, did not seem worried at all. “Clouds come and go,” she said. “The sky is patient, so we must be patient too.” On night duty at the hospital, when test results are slow to come back and everyone around me is in a hurry, I remember Dr Vân's words about the sky and try to wait calmly.

After reading · Talk about it

Give each answer as one paragraph that moves through the seven steps: Point → Why → How → Example → Result → Limitation → Evaluation.

1 · Why do people admire climbers like Messner even though the sport is so dangerous?

Model answer

PointI think we admire them not for the danger itself but for the way they deal with it. WhyMost of us would never take a risk like that, so someone who faces it calmly seems almost superhuman. HowReading about them, or watching them, lets us borrow a bit of that courage from the safety of the sofa. ExampleIn May 1996 the Swedish climber Göran Kropp turned round about a hundred metres below the top of Everest, simply because it was two in the afternoon and too late to get down safely. ResultTwenty days later he went back up and reached the summit, and in between, a storm on the mountain killed eight climbers. LimitationAdmittedly, the headlines usually go to the summits, not the turnarounds, so young climbers may copy the risks instead of the judgement. EvaluationEven so, the real draw, I'd say, is the years of training and the cool judgement behind every step they take.

2 · Was it right for Messner's father to take a five-year-old up a mountain?

Model answer

PointYes, as long as it was a mountain he knew well and the route was an easy one. WhyChildren come to love a place by being there, not by hearing about it years later. HowA careful parent picks a safe path, walks at the child's speed and turns back at the first sign of trouble. ExampleWhen I was six, my uncle took me up Bà Đen mountain in Tây Ninh, and I still remember eating sticky rice at the top while he pointed out the villages below. ResultThese days I'm the one in my family who organises every weekend trip to the hills. LimitationOf course, a small child can't explain clearly that they feel unwell, and high up that can be dangerous. EvaluationSo his father was right to start early, but anything really high should wait until a child can speak up for themselves.

3 · What makes someone ‘the greatest’ in their field: records, new ideas, or what other people say?

Model answer

PointFor me, new ideas count most, because records get broken and opinions change. WhyA record shows you were the best on one particular day, while a good idea keeps working long after you've stopped. HowYou can usually spot a great idea when, a few years later, nobody does things the old way any more. ExampleAt the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, Dick Fosbury won the high jump by going over the bar backwards, head first. ResultPeople laughed at first, but by the 1980 Olympics thirteen of the sixteen finalists were using his ‘Fosbury Flop’. LimitationTo be fair, nobody would've copied him if he hadn't won, so records still matter in a way. EvaluationThat's why Kammerlander's comment about Messner's new techniques tells me more than any list of summits.

4 · Should famous people write books about their own lives?

Model answer

PointYes, I think they should, but only if they're willing to be honest about the bad times. WhyNobody else knows what it felt like from the inside, and that's what readers want. HowThe best ones admit mistakes and fears instead of just listing trophies and achievements. ExampleIn Open, the tennis star Andre Agassi admitted that he had hated tennis for most of his career. ResultReaders were amazed, and the book reached number one on the New York Times bestseller list. LimitationThen again, many stars don't write the words themselves: Agassi wrote Open with a professional writer, J. R. Moehringer. EvaluationI'd still read books like that, just with the healthy doubt I'd bring to any story told by one side.

Before you watch (SB Ex 2): look at the painting of Voyager 1. Do you think it's important for humans to learn more about space with spacecraft like Voyager 1? Why? / Why not? The key words of SB Ex 1 (spacecraft, launched, solar system, mission, function, life forms, universe …) are on Sheet 3 · Group 3.

Watch (SB Ex 3–5). ▶ Part 1 (0:00–1:26) is for Questions 1–6 and ▶ Part 2 (1:27–4:37) for Questions 7–13; each button stops at the end of its part, and ⤢ plays the video full screen. Keep the transcript closed until you have answered.

Video + transcript | Questions

The transcript opens here when you press Show the transcript or Show answers.

Transcript

Hello from the children of planet Earth.Q1

That child's voice is a recorded message and the spacecraft Voyager 1 is currently carrying it further into space.Q1,Q6

The spacecraft Voyager 1 was launched on the 20th August, 1977. Its mission was to fly past the planets of Jupiter and Saturn and send back photographs to help scientists understand more about the two planets and our solar system.Q2

Over forty years later, Voyager 1 has completed its first mission successfully but it still has an important function.Q3

As well as sending messages back home, Voyager carries a message for other life forms in the universe.Q3,Q13 When scientists built Voyager 1, they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.Q4 It has different information about the Earth in 1977.

It was very difficult to choose what information to put on the record and so it took a team of six people nearly a year to decide.Q5

First of all, the team chose 116 photographs in black and white and in colour. These show pictures of Earth, pictures of human life including a human skeleton, a baby growing inside its mother and pictures of families.Q7,Q8 There are also photographs of animals and different places on Earth including cities, deserts and oceans.

Another part of the record is called ‘The sounds of Earth’.Q7 The twelve minutes of recording includes the sound of wind and rain, a volcano, birds and frogs, the human heart, and a child crying.Q9,Q10

Music was also important on the record and pieces were chosen to represent different parts of the world.Q7 There's classical music from Europe such as pieces by Bach and more modern jazz recordings by Louis Armstrong. There's also traditional music representing different cultures, from places like Azerbaijan, New Guinea, China, India and Peru.

And finally there are the recordings of human voices from Earth.Q7

Hello from the children of planet Earth. All the recordings are short messages with greetings in French, in Japanese, in Arabic and Mandarin Chinese.Q11

On screen‘Hello everybody.’ · ‘Hello? How are you?’ · ‘Greetings to our friends in the stars. We hope that we will meet you someday.’ · ‘Hope everyone's well. We are thinking about you all. Please come here and visit when you have the time.’Q11

In total, there are 55 different greetings in 55 different languages.

So as Voyager 1 finally leaves the Earth's solar system and travels into interstellar space, it carries a message with it.Q6,Q12 And who knows? Maybe someday someone — or something — will listen to the messages and send a reply.Q13

Fact note: NASA gives 5 September 1977 as Voyager 1's launch date; Voyager 2, launched on 20 August 1977, left first. The video has the two dates mixed up.

1Part 1. Who speaks the first words of the video?
1Part 1. Who speaks the first words of the video?
‘Hello from the children of planet Earth.’ Straight after it, the narrator explains: ‘That child's voice is a recorded message.’ So the very first words come from a child (SB Ex 4.1: true); the narrator only speaks second.Clue: 0:00 and 0:05: whose voice is it?
In the text: Hello from the children of planet Earth. That child's voice is a recorded message and the spacecraft Voyager 1 is currently carrying it further into space.
2According to the video, what was Voyager 1's mission when it set off?
2According to the video, what was Voyager 1's mission when it set off?
‘Its mission was to fly past the planets of Jupiter and Saturn and send back photographs …’ It flew past them and did not land; Mars and Venus are never mentioned, and the record was not the mission (SB Ex 4.2: true).Clue: 0:15–0:36: Its mission was to …
In the text: Its mission was to fly past the planets of Jupiter and Saturn and send back photographs to help scientists understand more about the two planets and our solar system.
3‘… it still has an important function.’ What does the narrator mean?
3‘… it still has an important function.’ What does the narrator mean?
but = the first job is finished, and yet the spacecraft still has a use. The next sentence says what: ‘As well as sending messages back home, Voyager carries a message for other life forms in the universe.’ Nothing says it is coming back or that the mission failed.Clue: 0:37–0:52: completed its first mission … but it still has an important function. As well as …
In the text: Over forty years later, Voyager 1 has completed its first mission successfully but it still has an important function. As well as sending messages back home, Voyager carries a message for other life forms in the universe.
4Where is the Golden Record?
4Where is the Golden Record?
‘When scientists built Voyager 1, they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.’ Fixed onto = attached to the outside (Video B, clip 2); around 1:00 you can see the gold disc beside the spacecraft. The video says nothing about the dish, the rocket, a capsule or Voyager 2.Clue: SB Ex 3.2: fixed … onto the side of.
In the text: When scientists built Voyager 1, they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.
5Who decided what to put on the record, and how long did it take them?
5Who decided what to put on the record, and how long did it take them?
‘it took a team of six people nearly a year to decide.’ Nearly a year = a little less than twelve months, so ‘six weeks’ and ‘over a year’ are both wrong, and the choosers were a team, not one scientist or a group of children.Clue: SB Ex 4.4: a number of people + a length of time.
In the text: It was very difficult to choose what information to put on the record and so it took a team of six people nearly a year to decide.
6What is Voyager 1 doing with the recorded message now?
6What is Voyager 1 doing with the recorded message now?
‘the spacecraft Voyager 1 is currently carrying it further into space’, and at the end it ‘travels into interstellar space’. It is moving away from us, so ‘travelling back to Earth’ (SB Ex 4.5) is false, and no planet is named as its goal. Voyager 1 does send its own data home by radio, but the record is fixed to the spacecraft and travels on with it.Clue: SB Ex 4.5: currently carrying it further into space.
In the text: That child's voice is a recorded message and the spacecraft Voyager 1 is currently carrying it further into space. So as Voyager 1 finally leaves the Earth's solar system and travels into interstellar space, it carries a message with it.
7Part 2. Which four kinds of material are on the Golden Record?

The narrator moves through ‘116 photographs’, ‘The sounds of Earth’, music chosen ‘to represent different parts of the world’ and ‘the recordings of human voices’. Films, maps, data and poems are not on the video's list.Clue: Part 2 has four sections: First of all → Another part → Music was also → And finally.
In the text: First of all, the team chose 116 photographs in black and white and in colour. These show pictures of Earth, pictures of human life including a human skeleton, a baby growing inside its mother and pictures of families. Another part of the record is called “The sounds of Earth”. Music was also important on the record and pieces were chosen to represent different parts of the world. And finally there are the recordings of human voices from Earth.
8What could the photographs of a human skeleton and a baby growing inside its mother tell a visitor from another world?
8What could the photographs of a human skeleton and a baby growing inside its mother tell a visitor from another world?
The photographs show ‘pictures of human life including a human skeleton, a baby growing inside its mother and pictures of families’. An ordinary photo shows our outside; only these show the inside of the body and the start of a new life. Nothing in the video is about illness, doctors on the team or how long people live.Clue: Inference: a visitor from another world has never seen a human body.
In the text: First of all, the team chose 116 photographs in black and white and in colour. These show pictures of Earth, pictures of human life including a human skeleton, a baby growing inside its mother and pictures of families.
9SB Exercise 5.2: in which order do you hear these sounds? a a human heart · b a child crying · c birds and frogs · d wind and rain · e a volcano
9SB Exercise 5.2: in which order do you hear these sounds? a a human heart · b a child crying · c birds and frogs · d wind and rain · e a volcano
‘the sound of wind and rain, a volcano, birds and frogs, the human heart, and a child crying’: d → e → c → a → b. The pictures follow the same order: a tree in the wind, a volcano, frogs, a heart, a crying baby.Clue: SB Ex 5.2: follow the list at 2:04–2:51.
In the text: The twelve minutes of recording includes the sound of wind and rain, a volcano, birds and frogs, the human heart, and a child crying.
10‘The sounds of Earth’ end with a human heart and a child crying. What is the most likely reason for choosing them?
10‘The sounds of Earth’ end with a human heart and a child crying. What is the most likely reason for choosing them?
After ‘wind and rain, a volcano, birds and frogs’ the record turns to us: ‘the human heart, and a child crying’. A heartbeat says ‘alive’, and a cry is one of the first sounds a person makes, a feeling without words. Loudness, doctors and quiet sounds are never mentioned, and twelve minutes leaves room for many more sounds.Clue: Purpose: the list moves from nature (wind, a volcano, animals) to people.
In the text: The twelve minutes of recording includes the sound of wind and rain, a volcano, birds and frogs, the human heart, and a child crying.
11SB Exercise 5.3: which greeting and language are matched correctly?
11SB Exercise 5.3: which greeting and language are matched correctly?
‘greetings in French, in Japanese, in Arabic and Mandarin Chinese’, and on screen: ‘Hello everybody.’ (French), ‘Hello? How are you?’ (Japanese), ‘Greetings to our friends in the stars …’ (Arabic), ‘Hope everyone's well …’ (Mandarin Chinese).Clue: SB Ex 5.3: the four English lines appear in the same order as the languages.
In the text: All the recordings are short messages with greetings in French, in Japanese, in Arabic and Mandarin Chinese. “Hello everybody.” · “Hello? How are you?” · “Greetings to our friends in the stars. We hope that we will meet you someday.” · “Hope everyone's well. We are thinking about you all. Please come here and visit when you have the time.”
12‘… leaves the Earth's solar system and travels into interstellar space.’ What is interstellar space?
12‘… leaves the Earth's solar system and travels into interstellar space.’ What is interstellar space?
The spacecraft first ‘leaves the Earth's solar system’, so interstellar space lies outside it, between our Sun and the other stars. The Moon, Jupiter and Saturn are all inside the solar system, and the word says nothing about photographs.Clue: Word parts: inter- = between (as in international); stellar = of the stars.
In the text: So as Voyager 1 finally leaves the Earth's solar system and travels into interstellar space, it carries a message with it.
13‘And who knows? Maybe someday someone — or something — will listen …’ How does the narrator feel at the end?
13‘And who knows? Maybe someday someone — or something — will listen …’ How does the narrator feel at the end?
‘And who knows? Maybe someday someone — or something — will listen to the messages and send a reply.’ He hopes for an answer but admits that nobody can know, and or something leaves room for a life form nothing like us. He never says a reply is certain, late or dangerous.Clue: And who knows? = nobody can be sure; Maybe someday = possibly, at a time nobody knows.
In the text: As well as sending messages back home, Voyager carries a message for other life forms in the universe. And who knows? Maybe someday someone — or something — will listen to the messages and send a reply.

Video B · Words in context · Video 11.2 · SB p. 139 Ex 6

After you watch (SB Ex 6): play each clip and choose the meaning of the word in bold. After each clip the video shows the book's question and then its answer, so use the clip buttons: they stop before the question screen, and you choose from the six meanings here.

Video + transcript | Questions

The transcript opens here when you press Show the transcript or Show answers.

Transcript

That child's voice is a recorded messageQ1 and the spacecraft Voyager 1 is currently carrying it further into space.

When scientists built Voyager 1, they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.Q2

Music was also important on the record and pieces were chosen to represent different parts of the world.Q3

All the recordings are short messages with greetings …Q4

Greetings to our friends in the stars. We hope that we will meet you someday.Q5 (on screen)

1Clip 1. ‘That child's voice is a recorded message …’ What does recorded mean here?
1Clip 1. ‘That child's voice is a recorded message …’ What does recorded mean here?
A recorded message is kept on a disc, a tape or a file, so it can be played again years later. That is how a child's voice from 1977 can still be travelling through space; it is not live, and it is not sent by radio.Clue: SB Ex 6.1 · TB key: put into a permanent form.
In the text: That child's voice is a recorded message
2Clip 2. ‘… they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.’ What does fixed onto mean?
2Clip 2. ‘… they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.’ What does fixed onto mean?
Fix X onto Y = join X firmly to Y so that it stays there. The record is attached to the outside of the spacecraft; nobody plays, changes or paints it there.Clue: SB Ex 6.2 · TB key: attached.
In the text: they fixed a golden record onto the side of the spacecraft.
3Clip 3. ‘… pieces were chosen to represent different parts of the world.’ What does represent mean?
3Clip 3. ‘… pieces were chosen to represent different parts of the world.’ What does represent mean?
Music from Europe, New Guinea, China, India and Peru stands for those parts of the world: it is a sign of them. The pieces are not copies of the places, and nothing is sold.Clue: SB Ex 6.3 · TB key: symbolize.
In the text: Music was also important on the record and pieces were chosen to represent different parts of the world.
4Clip 4. ‘All the recordings are short messages with greetings …’ What are greetings?
4Clip 4. ‘All the recordings are short messages with greetings …’ What are greetings?
A greeting is what you say when you meet someone: ‘Hello everybody.’, ‘Hello? How are you?’. Every message on the record opens with a friendly hello, not a warning, a thank-you or an apology.Clue: SB Ex 6.4 · TB key: words or signs of welcome.
In the text: All the recordings are short messages with greetings …
5Clip 5. ‘We hope that we will meet you someday.’ What does someday mean?
5Clip 5. ‘We hope that we will meet you someday.’ What does someday mean?
Someday = on a day that nobody knows yet. The speakers cannot know when, or even whether, anyone will find the record, so it cannot mean a fixed day or very soon.Clue: SB Ex 6.5 · TB key: at some time in the future.
In the text: We hope that we will meet you someday.
