Read the short biography and choose the best option for each gap

A biography with the parts SB 11e Ex 2 lists: birth and early life, why he became famous, what people say about him, his legacy.

Tôn Thất Tùng: the surgeon who made liver operations safer

Tôn Thất Tùng (1) passive was born + place + date in Thanh Hóa province on 10 May 1912, and he (2) his childhood in Huế, finished → past grew up in Huế. In 1935, (3) born 1912, so 23 in 1935 → in his early twenties; the early twenties would mean the 1920s, he started at the medical school in Hà Nội, and over the next four years he carefully cut open more than 200 livers from dead bodies to map their blood vessels. His thesis on this work won a prize in 1939.

In those days, many patients died during liver operations because they lost too much blood. In the 1960s Tùng developed a new (4) a new way of operating that surgeons learn → technique: the surgeon finds and ties off the blood vessels inside the liver before (5) before + ‑ing it, so far less blood is lost. Surgeons in other countries soon began to use it, and it (6) become known as + its name ‘Tung’s method’.

During the war against the French, he treated wounded soldiers at the resistance bases in the north and trained young doctors there. Later he ran Việt Đức Hospital in Hà Nội for almost thirty years. He (7) in 1982 → past simple died in Hà Nội in 1982, but he is still described as a (8) one of the first to do it → a pioneer of liver surgery, and his (9) what he left behind → his legacy (singular, lives) lives on in the surgeons he trained. In 1996, fourteen years after his death, he (10) someone gave him the prize → past passive was awarded the Hồ Chí Minh Prize.

Exercise 18 · Writing — put the advantages–disadvantages paragraph in order

Exercise 18

Put the ten sentences in order: give each one its number from 1 to 10

One paragraph on Sheet 8's Frame C (both sides, weighed): topic sentence · point 1, the lighter side · explanation · example · result · the turn + point 2, the heavier side · explanation · example · result · a concluding sentence that weighs the two sides. The linking words and the words that point back (this, that, those, the) fix the order.
The question

What are the advantages and disadvantages of keeping a hospital logbook only on a phone?

On the other hand, a logbook on a phone alone can disappear in a moment.
This is because cadets carry their phones everywhere, while a paper logbook is usually left in a locker.
Because of this, the cadet may have to repeat part of the placement.
Keeping a hospital logbook only on a phone has both clear benefits and serious drawbacks.
On balance, the risk of losing a placement's records outweighs the convenience of a phone logbook.
As a result, those two lines are more accurate than notes written later from memory.
The biggest benefit is that cadets can record each case as soon as it ends.
For instance, if a cadet's phone with no backup is stolen near the end of a placement, every checked case is gone.
For example, between patients on a ward there is no time to reach that locker, but there is time to type two lines.
The reason is that phones are easily lost or stolen, and few cadets make a backup.
The paragraph, sentence by sentence · linking words marked

1Keeping a hospital logbook only on a phone has both clear benefits and serious drawbacks.

1 · Topic sentence. The topic + has both … and …; the lighter side (benefits) is named first.

2The biggest benefit is that cadets can record each case as soon as it ends.

2 · Point 1 (the lighter side). The biggest benefit is that opens the side named first in the topic sentence.

3This is because cadets carry their phones everywhere, while a paper logbook is usually left in a locker.

3 · Explanation of point 1. This is because says why cases can be recorded at once (sentence 2).

4For example, between patients on a ward there is no time to reach that locker, but there is time to type two lines.

4 · Example of point 1. that locker is the one in sentence 3.

5As a result, those two lines are more accurate than notes written later from memory.

5 · Result of the example. those two lines are the ones typed in sentence 4.

6On the other hand, a logbook on a phone alone can disappear in a moment.

6 · The turn to the heavier side. On the other hand moves from the benefit to the drawback.

7The reason is that phones are easily lost or stolen, and few cadets make a backup.

7 · Explanation of point 2. The reason is that says why the logbook can disappear (sentence 6).

8For instance, if a cadet's phone with no backup is stolen near the end of a placement, every checked case is gone.

8 · Example of point 2. with no backup picks up the backup problem of sentence 7 and brings in one cadet.

9Because of this, the cadet may have to repeat part of the placement.

9 · Result of the example. the cadet is the one whose phone was stolen in sentence 8.

10On balance, the risk of losing a placement's records outweighs the convenience of a phone logbook.

10 · Weighing concluding sentence. On balance … outweighs puts the heavier side first and adds nothing new.

Exercise 19 · Speaking — a 7-step answer, step by step

Exercise 19

Recommend one life story for the academy library: choose the sentence for each step

Situation

The academy library has money for one life story for cadets this year: a book or a documentary. The librarian asks Class K84 to recommend one of these three.

The librarian asks you: ‘Which one should we buy, and why?’

1📘When Breath Becomes AirPaul Kalanithi · a young neurosurgeon's memoir · book · English and Vietnamese editions
2📗Do No HarmHenry Marsh · a brain surgeon looks back on nearly thirty years · book
3🎬Free SoloAlex Honnold climbs El Capitan without ropes · documentary · about 100 minutes
  • Choose one life story
  • Give your main reason
  • Say why the other two are less useful for cadets
  • 1' prepare · 2' speak

Build the model first: for each of the seven steps, pick the sentence that does that step's job. Then hide it and give your own answer, about another choice if you prefer.

Point
Point: the choice in one short sentence, nothing more.
Why
Why: the main reason, linked to the listeners (doctors in training).
How
How: the practical side: which editions to buy and how cadets would use them.
Example
Example: one real reader and one moment in the book.
Result
Result: what changed for that same reader afterwards.
Limitation
Limitation: Admittedly …, but … is fair to the other two choices, then answers them.
Evaluation
Evaluation: the final judgement from a new angle (what a library copy is for), not the Point or the Why again.
Model answer

PointIf the library can only afford one, I'd pick When Breath Becomes Air. WhyMainly, it's because Paul Kalanithi was still a doctor in training when he found out he had cancer, so he shows what happens when a doctor suddenly becomes the patient. HowThe library could buy the English original and the Vietnamese translation side by side, so cadets can read it in either language and practise their English at the same time. ExampleMy roommate read it on a field exercise last spring, and the chapter where Kalanithi looks at his own scans kept him awake half the night. ResultThe book changed him: he's kept a short notebook on every placement since then, and he says it's inspired him to listen to patients' fears, not just their symptoms. LimitationAdmittedly, Free Solo is more exciting and you can watch it in under two hours, and Do No Harm tells you far more about real operations, but one is about climbing, not medicine, and the other looks back on a thirty-year career we haven't even started. EvaluationOn balance, it's the book cadets will pass from hand to hand and still talk about in ten years, and that's exactly what a library copy is for.

In her free time she learned to jump with a parachute, and in 1962 this skill helped her to become one of five women chosen to train as cosmonauts.

Take off your hat, I’m (5) her ! goes inside the closing mark; nothing after it In almost three days she went round Earth 48 times, and she is still the only woman (6) the only woman to + perfect infinitive have flown a space mission alone. 1the passive phrase for the day and place a life began (be + past participle)

a turning point in someone’s life or career

a climber · a mountaineer
a climber /ˈklaɪmə(r)/
anyone who goes up rocks, walls, trees or hills
My roommate goes up the rocks by the reservoir every Saturday; he’s the best climber I know.
a mountaineer /ˌmaʊntəˈnɪə(r)/
someone who spends weeks high up on snow and ice, with ropes, tents and special tools
The mountaineers spent three weeks on the glacier before the weather let them try for the top.
✗ My little brother is a mountaineer: he goes up the mango tree every day. (→ climber)
be born · grow up
be born /bi ˈbɔːn/
the moment a life starts; always passive
I was born at home during a power cut, because the road to the hospital had flooded.
grow up /ˌɡrəʊ ˈʌp/
spend your childhood somewhere and become an adult; never passive
She grew up by the sea and could swim before she could read.
✗ I was grown up in the countryside. (→ grew up)
achieve · reach
achieve /əˈtʃiːv/
succeed in a goal you have worked hard for
She achieved her dream of studying medicine at the age of thirty.
reach /riːtʃ/
arrive at a place, a person or a level
The supply truck reached the border post just before dark.
✗ After a long climb, they achieved the old fort on the ridge. (→ reached)
a career · a job
a career /kəˈrɪə(r)/
all the working years a person spends in one field
In a thirty-year career, she ran field clinics in four provinces.
a job /dʒɒb/
the paid work you do now; one position
My first job was night porter at a small private clinic.
✗ He had a long and successful job as a mountain guide. (→ career)
dangerous · in danger
dangerous /ˈdeɪndʒərəs/
likely to hurt you
Loose rocks make the north side of the mountain dangerous.
in danger /ɪn ˈdeɪndʒə(r)/
likely to be hurt; describes the people at risk
When the snow started to slide, the whole team was in danger.
✗ We were very dangerous when the storm came. (→ in danger)
lose · miss
lose (lost, lost) /luːz/
no longer have something or someone
She lost her father in a road accident when she was six.
miss /mɪs/
feel sad that someone or something is not with you
During the expedition, he missed his children terribly.
✗ He missed three toes in the accident. (→ lost)
die · dead · death
die (died) /daɪ/
verb: stop living
Her grandfather died peacefully at ninety-one.
dead /ded/
adjective: no longer alive or working
The tree outside the clinic has been dead for years.
death /deθ/
noun: the end of a life
His brother’s death in the mountains changed the rest of his life.
✗ His brother was died on the mountain. (→ died)
in her twenties · at twenty
in his / her twenties /ɪn hɪz ˈtwentiz/
during the ten years from age 20 to 29
In his twenties, my father drove an ambulance in the Central Highlands.
at twenty /ət ˈtwenti/ · at the age of twenty
exactly at that age
My father joined the army at nineteen.
✗ He got married in the age of twenty-four. (→ at the age of)
2b
Which one, and why?
7′
1 · After eleven hours on the ice, the rescue team finally ____ the injured climber.
reached: reach + a person or a place, with no preposition. You achieve a goal, and arrive needs at.
2 · My father ____ on a tea farm, picking leaves every morning until he was fifteen.
grew up: the sentence covers years of childhood. Be born is one moment, and grow up is never passive.
3 · Many people respect her, but among climbers she is more than that: she’s a ____.
legend: after a we need a noun for a person. Legendary is an adjective; a legacy is what someone leaves behind.
4 · She ____ the hearing in one ear after a fall on the ice.
lost: after the fall she no longer has that hearing. Miss is about feeling sad that someone is away, and die takes no object.
5 · The rope bridge was so old that crossing it was ____.
dangerous: crossing it could hurt you. In danger describes the people at risk, and danger is a noun.
6 · Over a long ____, she worked in six different military hospitals.
career: the whole working life she spent in hospitals. One job cannot cover six of them, and work is uncountable, so no a.
7 · Sadly, his younger brother ____ in a car crash at twenty.
died: an active verb in the past simple. Dead is an adjective, and was died does not exist.
8 · My grandmother learned to read ____ sixty-two, and now she reads the news aloud to us.
at + an exact age. In her sixties would also be right, but in her sixty-two is not.

Choose and correct

Active · with help⏱ 10 min
GoalUse the words for a life and a climb accurately, and correct sentences that get them wrong.
3a
Fix the sentence
5′

The underlined part of each sentence is wrong. Choose the correct version from the list.

1My great-grandfather born in 1921, the year his village built its first school.
→
Be born is passive, and a finished year needs the past simple: was born.
2The young surgeon is famous for discover a faster way to close wounds.
→
After the preposition for, use the ‑ing form: famous for discovering.
3After a long night on the ridge, our team leader achieved the summit alone.
→
You reach a place such as a summit; achieve goes with goals and dreams, and arrive needs at.
4‘You can rest when you get to the top,’ said she, and smiled.
→
After a quote, write she said or said + a name (said Lan); said she sounds old-fashioned, and told needs a listener.
5People in the valley have always described the old guide like a living map.
→
describe someone as + what people say they are; like is wrong after describe.
6Two climbers were died in an avalanche last winter.
→
Die is an active verb, and last winter needs the past simple: died.
7When I was a teenager, I have climbed the hill behind our school almost every Sunday.
→
When I was a teenager is a finished time, so the past simple: climbed.
8Climbing alone with no rope means taking a huge risky.
→
After a huge we need a singular noun: take a risk. Risky is the adjective.
9Grandpa was the first man in his unit learned to drive a truck.
→
The first (person, woman, man) + to + base verb: the first man to learn.
10We set off at 3 a.m. because the afternoon storms make the ridge danger.
→
make + something + an adjective: the storms make the ridge dangerous. Danger is a noun.
3b
Complete Minh’s biography of his grandmother
5′

My grandmother, Đặng Thị Lan, (1) be born is always passive, and 1948 is finished: was born in 1948 in a small village in the hills of central Vietnam. (2) As a teenager = when she was a teenager; since would need a full clause and a perfect tense a teenager, she carried rice and medicine up mountain paths for the soldiers. In her (3) in her twenties = between 20 and 29, she trained as a midwife, and she (4) go on to + base verb shows the next step in a life; the story is in the past, so went deliver more than two thousand babies. People in the district still describe her (5) describe someone as + a description ‘the woman who never slept’. (6) the verb spends is present simple, so the time phrase must be about now, she spends her mornings in her vegetable garden and her afternoons telling stories to her great-grandchildren.

Make your own sentences

From notes to sentences

Turn each line of notes into one full sentence. Say it out loud, then compare it with the two models.

Mekong Delta · market town · 1990 · born · grow up · help · mother · noodle stall

Models

1She grew up in a Mekong Delta market town, where she was born in 1990, helping her mother run a noodle stall.

2She came into the world in 1990 in a small Delta town and spent her childhood washing bowls at her mother’s noodle stall.

as a teenager · climb · every weekend · older brother · in his twenties · join · mountain rescue team

Models

1As a teenager, he climbed every weekend with his older brother, and in his twenties he joined a mountain rescue team.

2Weekends in his teens meant climbing with his big brother; then, in his twenties, he signed up for mountain rescue.

2015 · fall · break · both legs · doctors · say · never climb again · two years later · reach · summit

Models

1In 2015 she fell and broke both legs, and the doctors said she would never climb again, but two years later she reached the summit.

2Her doctors were sure that a fall in 2015, which broke both her legs, had ended her climbing; two years on, she stood on the summit.

famous for · set up · first free clinic · district · describe as · local hero

Models

1He is famous for setting up the first free clinic in the district, and people have described him as a local hero.

2Opening the district’s first free clinic made his name, and to this day people describe him as a local hero.

4b
Make it true for you
5′

Complete each frame so it is true about your life, with at least one Tier 2 chunk. Then read the two examples.

The person I admire most is … because …

Examples

1The person I admire most is my primary school teacher, Mrs Hằng, because she taught forty children in one room and still knew every one of our birthdays.

2The person I admire most is my older sister, because she went back to university at thirty while working night shifts in a pharmacy.

A turning point in my life was … After that, I …

Examples

1A turning point in my life was the night my grandfather had a stroke. After that, I gave up the idea of engineering and started reading biology books.

2A turning point in my life was my first week of military training. After that, I never complained about getting up early again.

The highest place I’ve ever been to is … To get there, we …

Examples

1The highest place I’ve ever been to is the top of Fansipan. To get there, we took the cable car and then walked up the last few hundred steps to the summit.

2The highest place I’ve ever been to is a border post at about 1,800 metres. To get there, we drove for six hours and then carried our packs up a muddy track for two more.

Step 5 / 6 · Produce

Speak, upgrade, then try a new task

Active · freely⏱ 18 min
GoalTell a 20-second life story with one quote, upgrade it with the 7-step frame, then introduce a guest speaker.
5a
Upgrade my answer
8′
Speaking task · a 20-second biography

‘Tell the group about someone you admire: who they are, the key moments of their life and why they matter to you. Include one thing they said, in direct speech.’

Talk for about 20 seconds with Tier 1 words: who the person is, where they were born and why you admire them. Finish with one quote.

Example

My hero is my uncle Thành. He was born on a rice farm and trained as an army doctor at twenty-three. These days he runs a tiny clinic up in the mountains, and I admire him because he has never once asked to come home. ‘A doctor walks first and complains later,’ he likes to say.

Now tell it through the 7-step frame, adding two Tier 2 chunks; keep each step to one short sentence.

Example

PointPeople in his district have described my uncle Thành as their lifeline. WhyHe turned down a comfortable hospital job in the city to work there. HowEvery week he hikes to villages that have no clinic of their own. ExampleLast winter, with the pass closed by ice, he took a real risk and drove an old man with pneumonia down to hospital himself. ResultThe old man pulled through, and now he sends my uncle a bag of tea every spring. LimitationThe pay is poor, though, and his knees are starting to complain. EvaluationEven so, his life has convinced me that I picked the right career.

Choose one follow-up question and answer it in about 20 seconds.

  • What would you ask this person if you were writing their biography?
  • Is it better to admire famous people or people you know?
Example

I’d ask my uncle about the nights when things went wrong. He only ever tells us the happy endings, and a biography that left out the failures would be half a life.

Read the model and find each of the seven steps.

PointIf you asked me who I admire most, I wouldn’t name anyone famous: I’d name my uncle Thành. WhyThe main reason is that he chose the hardest life on offer when an easy one was waiting for him in Hanoi. HowAfter graduating, he asked for a posting in the far north-west, and he still carries his medical bag on foot to hamlets that have never seen a car. ExampleTake one night in 2018, when a woman went into labour two hours away and the only path crossed a stream that was rising fast. ResultHe waded over with his bag above his head, and by morning there was a healthy baby boy, who now carries my uncle’s name. LimitationAdmittedly, his own children saw him only a few times a year. EvaluationStill, I’d rate a life like his above any record set on a mountain. ‘Somebody has to go,’ he once told me, ‘so why not me?’

Hide the model and tell the life story again in 60–90 seconds: all seven steps, plus your quote.

5b
New situation · introduce a guest speaker
10′
Task · spoken introduction · 45–60 seconds

Imagine the academy has invited a mountain rescue doctor, Dr Hà, to speak to 300 cadets, and you must introduce her. These are the notes on her speaker card.

  • born 1979 · village near Sa Pa · mother / village nurse
  • as a teenager / guided tourists on mountain paths
  • first job / border clinic / four hours’ walk from the road
  • 2014 / led a team / brought six injured climbers down in a storm
  • her sayings: patient / can’t come to you / so you go to the patient · mountain / doesn’t care / your plans · pack / for your worst day / not your best
  1. Say who she is and why the cadets should listen to her.
  2. Tell her story in order and quote one of her sayings in direct speech.
1:00Tap every chunk you use.
🚀 Challenge card

Do at least two:

  • use was born and one more life-story pattern (went on to, has worked)
  • punctuate the quote correctly (quotation marks, a comma, she says or says Dr Hà)
  • use has been described as or famous for + ‑ing
  • add one climbing chunk (take a risk, reach the summit)
Suggested answers · 3 levels
● Core

Who she isGood afternoon, everyone. Our guest today is Dr Hà, a mountain rescue doctor. Dr Hà comes from a village near Sa Pa; she was born there in 1979. Her mother was the village nurse.

Her storyAs a teenager, she guided tourists on the mountain paths. Her first job was at a clinic near the border. In 2014 her team saved six climbers in a terrible storm. She always says, ‘The patient can’t come to you, so you go to the patient.’

●● Stretch

Who she isPlease welcome a doctor who has spent most of her life above the clouds. Dr Hà grew up near Sa Pa, following her mother, the only nurse for miles, from house to house.

Her storyShe started work at a border clinic that you could only reach on foot, and she went on to lead a rescue team. In 2014 that team carried six injured climbers down through a storm. ‘The mountain doesn’t care about your plans,’ she says. That’s why she always makes three.

●●● Challenge

Who she isIt’s an honour to introduce today’s speaker, who has been described as a legend among rescue teams. Her mother nursed a whole valley near Sa Pa, and as a teenager Dr Hà was already leading tourists up paths most of us couldn’t even find.

Her storyShe became famous for one night in 2014, when she took a huge risk and brought six injured climbers down in a storm that had stopped every helicopter. Ask her how she did it and she’ll just smile. ‘Pack for your worst day, not your best,’ says Dr Hà. So please, get your questions ready.

Step 1 / 6 · Notice

Meet the words

Passive · understand⏱ 12 min
GoalUnderstand the space and recording words, and use them to talk about Voyager 1 and the Golden Record.
1a
Look and describe
3′
1b
Choose: active or passive?
3′

Choose the form that fits each sentence, then press Check. A short reason appears under every item.

1The first satellite into space by the Soviet Union in 1957.
by the Soviet Union names who did it, so the passive: was launched.
2Every Friday, our anatomy lecturer her talk for cadets on night duty.
The lecturer does the action, and her talk is the object: active.
3Thousands of photos back by the probe since it left Earth.
Photos cannot send themselves; by the probe shows the passive.
4In the drawing, a small circle the Sun.
The circle stands for the Sun, which is the object: active present simple.
5On the poster, each country by its flag.
The flag is the sign and the country is shown by it: passive with by.
6The nurse a name band to every newborn’s wrist.
The nurse does it to the name band: active.
7A short greeting in Vietnamese first and then in English.
A greeting cannot record itself; someone recorded it: passive.
8Scientists the mission a success after the last photos arrived.
The scientists did the calling, and the mission is the object: active.
9Our platoon by the director to choose ten photos for the time capsule.
by the director shows who did the asking, so the passive: was asked.
10The team every song with great care.
The team did the choosing, and every song is the object: active.

Meaning, check questions, form
6′

Read each example sentence and answer both check questions aloud. Tap a question to see the answer.

launch /lɔːntʃ/

Our physics club launched a water rocket that flew higher than the academy flagpole.

Check questions
✓ launch a satellite · be launched into space✗ be launched into the space
a mission /ə ˈmɪʃn/

Check questions
✓ complete a mission✗ make a mission
represent /ˌreprɪˈzent/

On the evacuation map, each red cross represents a field hospital.

Check questions
✓ The cross represents a hospital.✗ The cross is represented a hospital.
a greeting /ə ˈɡriːtɪŋ/

The old guard’s greeting never changed: a quick salute and a wide smile.

✓ send greetings to …✗ send greets to …

Step 2 / 6 · Tell apart

Pairs that look alike

Passive → active⏱ 15 min
GoalTell apart space and message words that are easy to confuse, and explain your choice.
2a
Compare the pairs
8′

Read both sides of every card. Then cover them, tap the quick test and answer it.

space · the space
space /speɪs/
no article: everything outside the Earth’s atmosphere; also ‘room’, uncountable
Satellites in space can see a storm long before it reaches land.
the space · a space /ðə speɪs/
one particular empty area
Put your boots in the space under the bed.
✗ Every year, more satellites are sent into the space. (→ into space)
a planet · a star · a moon
a planet /ˈplænɪt/
a big round world of rock or gas that moves around a star
Saturn is the planet with the famous rings.
a star /stɑː(r)/
a giant, very hot object in space that shines with its own light
The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system.
a moon /muːn/
a natural object that travels round a planet
Earth has only one moon.
✗ The Sun is the biggest planet in our sky. (→ star)
explore · discover
explore /ɪkˈsplɔː(r)/
go through an unfamiliar place and look at everything in it
The students explored the hospital’s old tunnels with a torch.
discover /dɪˈskʌvə(r)/
come across something nobody knew about, or find out a new fact
In 1610, Galileo discovered four moons going round Jupiter.
✗ We discovered the night market for two hours before dinner. (→ explored)
a record · a recording
a record /ˈrekɔːd/
a flat disc with sound on it; also the best result ever
Dad still keeps a box of his parents’ old records under the stairs.
a recording /rɪˈkɔːdɪŋ/
sound or pictures stored on any device
There’s a recording of every lecture on the academy website.
✗ Listen to this record I made of the rain on my phone. (→ recording)
a satellite · a spacecraft · a probe
a satellite /ˈsætəlaɪt/
anything that goes round a planet; most are machines for weather, phones or TV
Weather satellites send new pictures of the clouds many times a day.
a spacecraft /ˈspeɪskrɑːft/
a vehicle that a rocket carries beyond our planet, crewed or not
The spacecraft carried three astronauts to the space station.
a probe /prəʊb/
an unmanned machine sent on a long trip to gather data
In 1989, a probe with no one on board flew past Neptune.
✗ Voyager 1 is a satellite of the Earth. (→ a probe: it does not go round the Earth)
someday · one day
someday /ˈsʌmdeɪ/
future only, with no date in mind
Someday I’ll take my parents to see the sea at Phú Quốc.
one day /ˈwʌn deɪ/
on a certain date in the past, or at some point in the future
One day last spring, a parcel arrived with no name on it.
✗ Someday last week I lost my student card. (→ One day)
represent · present
represent /ˌreprɪˈzent/
be the symbol of something; or speak officially for a team or a country
Each candle on the cake represents ten years of the academy.
present /prɪˈzent/
show or give something formally to an audience
Each group will present its plan in five minutes.
✗ Tomorrow I will represent my research to the professors. (→ present)
classical · classic
classical /ˈklæsɪkl/
the serious, centuries-old Western style of composers like Mozart
My roommate falls asleep to classical music every night.
classic /ˈklæsɪk/
excellent and typical; still loved many years later
Tom and Jerry is a classic cartoon.
✗ My father only listens to classic music. (→ classical)
2b
Which one, and why?
7′
1 · Weather forecasts depend on ____ that go round the Earth day and night.
satellites travel round the Earth all the time; a probe heads far away, and planets go round the Sun.
2 · There was no ____ left in the lecture hall, so we stood at the back.
space here means room, an uncountable noun, so no article after no.
3 · Last weekend our platoon spent four hours ____ the caves near the border with a local guide.
exploring: four hours spent going through the caves and looking around. Discover is one moment of finding something new, and nobody invents caves.
4 · The police listened to a ____ of the phone call again and again.
recording: the stored sound of the call. A recorder is the machine, and a record is a disc or a best result.
5 · In Vietnamese art, the lotus flower often ____ purity.
represents: the flower is a sign that stands for purity. Present means show formally, and prevent means stop.
6 · I wrote to the space museum in March, and their ____ came only last week.
reply: their answer to my letter. A greeting is a hello, and a mission is a task.
7 · The orchestra will play ____ music by Beethoven and Tchaikovsky at the New Year concert.
classical music is the name of the style. Classic means excellent and long-loved; classy means stylish.
8 · A ____ with no crew can travel for decades and still send back data.
probe: a spacecraft without people. An astronaut is a person, and a solar system is not a vehicle.
Step 3 / 6 · Control

Choose and correct

Active · with help⏱ 10 min
GoalUse the space and recording words accurately, and correct the sentences that misuse them.
3a
Fix the sentence
5′

The underlined part of each sentence is wrong. Choose the correct version from the list.

1In 2019, a Japanese rocket was launched MicroDragon, a small satellite built by Vietnamese engineers.
→
The rocket did the launching and MicroDragon is the object, so the active past simple: launched.
2The probe is now heading out of solar system.
→
We mean our own, the only one around us, so it takes the and stays singular.
3As a science project, our club tried to beam a short signal to the space from the school roof.
→
Outer space takes no article, and movement out there is into space.
4This old photo is representing life in our village in the 1980s.
→
Represent describes a state here, so the present simple: represents.
5The rescue team did its mission in under three hours.
→
We complete (or carry out) a mission; do, make and take don’t go with it.
6My grandfather still listens to the jazz every evening.
→
A kind of music in general takes no article: listen to jazz, love classical music.
7She sent me a voice record instead of a text message.
→
What she sent was stored sound, so it is a voice recording; a record would be a disc or a best result.
8Thanks for the message; I’ll reply it tomorrow.
→
The verb reply needs to before the message or the person: reply to it.
9At the start of the video call, the children shouted their greets in three languages.
→
The noun is greeting, plural here because there were three languages: greetings.
10Someday last summer, our class found a box of letters under the library stairs.
→
Someday is only for the future; for a past event, use One day.

Hi everyone! The memory stick for the academy time capsule has (1) memory is uncountable, so lots of; many needs a plural noun, and a lot needs of digital memory, but let’s choose carefully. First, one photo of our morning drill should (2) one picture stands for the whole academy: represent the whole academy. Second, the director has agreed to give a short (3) an adjective before message: a recorded message is one that has been recorded message. Third, each of us will add a greeting (4) in + a language or a dialect our own home dialect. Lan also wants some (5) an adjective before the noun music music from her village. Who knows? The cadets of 2075 might even send us a (6) a + a singular noun: a reply!

From notes to sentences

Turn each line of notes into one full sentence. Say it out loud, then compare it with the two models.

1977 · two probes · launch · Florida · long tour · the giant planets

Models

every cadet · record · ten-second message · family · put · all · one memory stick

sounds · represent · our country · rain on a tin roof · temple bell · street market

4b
Make it true for you
5′

Complete each frame so it is true about your life, with at least one Tier 2 chunk. Then read the two examples.

If I could send one photo into space, it would show … because …

Examples

1If I could send one photo into space, it would show the market in my hometown at six in the morning, because it represents how busy and noisy we are.

2If I could send one photo into space, it would show a midwife holding a newborn baby, because that’s where every human story begins.

The sound that represents my hometown best is … because …

Examples

1The sound that represents my hometown best is the ferry horn at dawn, because the whole town wakes up to it.

2The sound that represents my hometown best is the call of the woman selling sticky rice, because I’ve heard it every morning of my life.

One question I’d like to ask an astronaut is … because …

Examples

1One question I’d like to ask an astronaut is how you treat a bleeding wound in space, because blood must behave very strangely without gravity.

2One question I’d like to ask an astronaut is what they missed most about Earth, because I suspect it would be something small, like the smell of rain.

Step 5 / 6 · Produce

Speak, upgrade, then try a new task

Active · freely⏱ 18 min
GoalPitch three things for a memory stick for space with the 7-step frame, then plan a message for a time capsule.
5a
Upgrade my answer
8′
Speaking task · a group pitch

‘Imagine your group works for a space agency. In 20 seconds, tell the other group the three things you would put on a memory stick for space, and why.’

Talk for about 20 seconds with Tier 1 words: name your three things and give one reason for the whole set.

Example

We’d choose three things. First, a clip of doctors working together in an operating theatre. Second, a lullaby that grandmothers sing in Vietnamese villages. And third, one minute of Hanoi’s traffic! Together they show how we live, how we care for each other and, honestly, how busy we are.

Now pitch it through the 7-step frame, adding two Tier 2 chunks; keep each step to one short sentence.

Example

PointEven with lots of digital memory, we’d keep it to three files: an operation, a lullaby and some city noise. WhyWe want to show how people live today, not only what our planet looks like. HowEvery file would be short, and none would need translating. ExampleThe lullaby is the one my grandmother sang to me every night when I was small. ResultAnyone who heard it would understand that we look after our young. LimitationThe traffic, on the other hand, might make Earth sound rather stressful. EvaluationStill, three real moments say more about us than a recorded message full of polite words.

Choose one follow-up question and answer it in about 20 seconds.

  • Who should decide what goes on the stick: scientists, artists or ordinary people?
  • Would you include anything sad, such as a photo from a war?
Example

Yes, at least one. A message with only smiling faces wouldn’t be the whole truth, and if anyone ever visits, they’ll learn about our wars anyway.

Read the model and find each of the seven steps.

PointIf our group were filling a memory stick for space, we’d put just three things on it: a video of a surgical team at work, a Vietnamese lullaby and a photo of my family round the table at Tết. WhyThe reason is that the Golden Record showed what Earth was like in 1977, and we’d like to show what people are like now. HowNone of the files would depend on words, so whoever finds the stick could follow them without knowing a single human language. ExampleFor instance, on my hospital placement last month I watched eight people work around one patient for five hours, passing instruments to each other without a word. ResultYou could tell from their hands alone that a life was being saved, and that’s exactly the moment we’d want to send. LimitationAdmittedly, an alien machine might not be able to open our video files at all. EvaluationEven so, if only one of the three plays, they’ll see that humans look after each other, and that’s the part of our story most worth sending.

Hide the model and give the pitch again in 60 seconds, moving through all seven steps.

5b
New situation · the academy time capsule
10′
Task · speak and write

The academy is filling a time capsule that cadets will open in 2075, and each platoon can add one memory stick. Your platoon has chosen you to speak for it.

  1. Speak · 45 seconds: present three things for the stick (a photo, a sound or video, and a recorded message) and say what each one represents.
  2. Write · 3 minutes: the recorded message itself, 4–5 sentences, with a greeting and one question for the cadets of 2075.
0:45Tap every chunk you use.
🚀 Challenge card

Do at least two:

  • use one passive (was recorded · was chosen · will be opened)
  • use represent + a noun
  • speak on behalf of your platoon
  • end your message with a question that invites a reply
Suggested answers · 3 levels
● Core

Our choicesOur platoon chose three things. The first is a picture of our platoon marching in the rain. The second is a video of the academy band. The third is a short message from all of us.

Our messageHello, cadets of 2075! We are Platoon 4. These days we study anatomy and work long night shifts. Do you still carry paper notebooks? We hope you can answer us someday.

●● Stretch

Our choicesWe’d like to put three things on the stick. First, a photo of forty tired cadets after a night exercise, because it represents how hard we work. Then a recording of one of our lectures, so you can hear how we were taught. Finally, a recorded message from the whole platoon.

Our messageGreetings from Platoon 4! This message was recorded in the library on a rainy Tuesday afternoon in 2026. We hope medicine is kinder and faster in your time. What is the biggest change in your training? Please leave your answer in the next capsule.

Our choicesOn behalf of Platoon 4, I’d like to present our three choices. The photo was chosen by a vote: it shows us carrying a stretcher up a muddy hill, and for us it symbolises teamwork. Next comes a two-minute video of a night shift, sound and all. And last, a greeting from each of us in the dialect of our home province.

Our messageGood morning, colleagues of 2075. By the time you hear this, most of us will be retired doctors, or old patients. Perhaps one of you will treat one of us someday. We only ask one thing: what did our generation get wrong? Write it down and keep it safe for the cadets who come after you.

GoalTalk about space and the Golden Record from memory, with your notes hidden.

Hide your notes, look at the picture and explain it in three sentences: what the gold disc is, where it is and why it is there.

Compare with a model

It’s a gold-plated copper record with sounds and pictures from Earth on it. It’s attached to Voyager 1 itself, which has travelled further from home than any other spacecraft. It’s there in case other life forms find the probe one day and want to know who sent it.

On our memory stick for space we would put ________. The first one represents ________. We would also include a recording of ________ because ________. Our recorded message would say, ‘________.’ Someday, ________.
